topics.topic: Branches of biology and scientific method
topics.summary: Biology is split into branches named mostly from Greek and Latin roots, and every branch advances by the same scientific method: observe, question, hypothesise, test, conclude. NSMQ riddles and rapid-fire rounds often ask for the name of a branch, the steps of the method, or the type of variable in a described experiment.
keyIdeas: The suffix -logy means 'study of'; the root in front tells you what is studied (cyto = cell, histo = tissue, myco = fungus).
The suffix -culture means rearing or cultivating for human use (apiculture = bees, sericulture = silkworms, pisciculture = fish).
A hypothesis is a testable, falsifiable explanation or prediction; it is supported or rejected by data, never 'proved'.
A theory is a broad, repeatedly tested explanation (cell theory, theory of evolution); a law describes a regular pattern without explaining it.
In a fair test only the independent variable is changed, the dependent variable is measured, and all other (controlled) variables are kept constant.
A control experiment is set up identically but without the factor under test, so any difference can be blamed on that factor.
Repeating trials and using larger samples increases reliability; accuracy is closeness to the true value, precision is closeness of repeats to each other.
Carl Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature: Genus (capital letter) + species (small letter), italicised in print or underlined separately when handwritten.

formulas.name: Steps of the scientific method
formulas.formula: Observation → problem/question → hypothesis → experiment → results (data) → analysis → conclusion → (theory)
formulas.note: If the results reject the hypothesis, a new hypothesis is formed and tested.

formulas.name: Types of variable
formulas.formula: Independent = changed by the experimenter; Dependent = measured; Controlled = kept constant
formulas.note: The independent variable goes on the x-axis, the dependent on the y-axis.

formulas.name: Mean of repeats
formulas.formula: x̄ = Σx / n
formulas.note: Exclude obvious anomalies before averaging; n is the number of valid readings.

formulas.name: Percentage change
formulas.formula: % change = (final − initial) / initial × 100
formulas.note: Used for growth, mass change in osmosis, population change. Negative means a decrease.

formulas.name: Taxonomic hierarchy
formulas.formula: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum (Division in plants) → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
formulas.note: Going down, organisms share more features; species is the basic unit of classification.

formulas.name: Binomial name
formulas.formula: Genus species, e.g. Homo sapiens, Zea mays, Plasmodium falciparum
formulas.note: Genus capitalised, species epithet lower case; the pair is italicised.

formulas.name: Branches named after organisms
formulas.formula: Zoology = animals; Botany = plants; Mycology = fungi; Phycology (algology) = algae; Bacteriology = bacteria; Virology = viruses; Entomology = insects; Ichthyology = fish; Herpetology = reptiles and amphibians; Ornithology = birds; Mammalogy = mammals
formulas.note: Microbiology covers bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists together.

formulas.name: Branches named after level or process
formulas.formula: Cytology = cells; Histology = tissues; Anatomy = internal structure; Morphology = form; Physiology = functions; Genetics = heredity; Ecology = organisms and environment; Embryology = development of embryos; Palaeontology = fossils; Ethology = animal behaviour; Taxonomy = classification; Limnology = fresh waters
formulas.note: Medical: haematology = blood, cardiology = heart, nephrology = kidneys, dermatology = skin, oncology = cancer, endocrinology = hormones.

formulas.name: Applied -culture branches
formulas.formula: Apiculture = bees; Sericulture = silkworms; Pisciculture = fish farming; Aquaculture = aquatic organisms; Horticulture = garden crops, fruits, flowers; Floriculture = flowers; Silviculture = forest trees; Viticulture = grapes; Olericulture = vegetables
formulas.note: Agriculture is the umbrella term; these are its specialisations.

shortcuts.name: Decode the root
shortcuts.rule: Translate the Greek or Latin root and add -logy: ichthys = fish, ornis = bird, herpeton = creeping animal, entomon = insect, mykes = fungus, phykos = seaweed, haima = blood, onkos = mass/tumour.
shortcuts.example: 'The study of birds?' ornis = bird → ornithology. 'Study of tumours?' onkos → oncology. Done in under 5 s.

shortcuts.name: Hierarchy mnemonic
shortcuts.rule: Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup = Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
shortcuts.example: 'Which rank lies between Class and Family?' Came Over For → Order.

shortcuts.name: 'Effect of X on Y' rule
shortcuts.rule: In any title of the form 'the effect of X on Y', X is the independent variable and Y is the dependent variable; everything else mentioned must be controlled.
shortcuts.example: 'Effect of temperature on the rate of yeast respiration' → independent = temperature, dependent = rate of CO₂ release, controlled = glucose concentration, yeast mass, volume.

shortcuts.name: Latin root for -culture
shortcuts.rule: apis = bee, sericum = silk, piscis = fish, silva = forest, vitis = vine, hortus = garden, flos/floris = flower, olus = vegetable.
shortcuts.example: 'Rearing of silkworms for silk?' sericum = silk → sericulture.

shortcuts.name: Percentage change by fractions
shortcuts.rule: Write the change over the original as a simple fraction you know: 1/4 = 25%, 1/5 = 20%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 3/4 = 75%.
shortcuts.example: Plant height goes from 40 cm to 50 cm: change 10/40 = 1/4 = 25% increase.

traps: Saying a hypothesis was 'proved'; data only support or reject it.
Confusing entomology (insects) with etymology (word origins).
Writing the species name with a capital letter (Homo Sapiens is wrong) or forgetting to italicise/underline.
Mixing up a control experiment (whole set-up lacking the test factor) with controlled variables (factors kept the same).
Thinking herpetology covers only snakes; it covers all reptiles and amphibians.
nsmqTips: Riddles often give clues like 'I study creatures that crawl... I include frogs too' — listen for the root organism and jump straight to the -logy word.
For experiment questions, name the variables using the 'effect of X on Y' rule first, then state the control.
When asked who did what: Linnaeus = binomial nomenclature, Robert Hooke = named cells (1665), Schleiden and Schwann = cell theory, Mendel = father of genetics, Darwin = natural selection.
Answer with the exact term (e.g. 'ichthyology'), not a description; quizmasters want the word.

topics.summary: The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living things, and each organelle has a specific job. NSMQ asks for organelle functions, plant versus animal and prokaryote versus eukaryote differences, and magnification calculations.
keyIdeas: Cell theory: all organisms are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Prokaryotes (bacteria, archaea) lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; they have 70S ribosomes, a nucleoid, often plasmids, and a peptidoglycan (murein) wall in bacteria.
Eukaryotes have a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes.
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, a large permanent vacuole with tonoplast, and chloroplasts; animal cells have centrioles, small temporary vacuoles and store glycogen instead of starch.
Double-membrane structures: nucleus (nuclear envelope), mitochondrion, chloroplast. Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes (evidence for endosymbiosis).
Rough ER (with ribosomes) makes and transports proteins; smooth ER makes lipids and steroids; Golgi body modifies, packages and secretes; lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes.
The plasma membrane follows the fluid mosaic model: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; it is partially (selectively) permeable.
Light microscopes resolve about 0.2 µm; electron microscopes resolve below 1 nm, so ribosomes and membrane detail are seen only with the electron microscope.

formulas.name: Magnification
formulas.formula: M = image size / actual size
formulas.note: Both sizes must be in the same unit. Rearranged: actual size = image size / M.

formulas.name: Total magnification (light microscope)
formulas.formula: Total M = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification
formulas.note: ×10 eyepiece with ×40 objective gives ×400.

formulas.name: Length units
formulas.formula: 1 m = 10³ mm = 10⁶ µm = 10⁹ nm; 1 mm = 1000 µm; 1 µm = 1000 nm
formulas.note: Typical sizes: animal cell 10–30 µm, bacterium 1–5 µm, mitochondrion 1–10 µm long, ribosome ≈ 20–30 nm.

formulas.name: Resolution
formulas.formula: Light microscope ≈ 0.2 µm (200 nm); transmission electron microscope ≈ 0.1–1 nm
formulas.note: Resolution is the smallest separation at which two points are seen as separate; magnification without resolution only gives a bigger blur.

formulas.name: Surface area to volume of a cube
formulas.formula: SA:V = 6L² / L³ = 6/L
formulas.note: As size increases, SA:V falls; this limits cell size and explains why large organisms need transport systems.

formulas.name: Ribosome sizes
formulas.formula: Prokaryotic 70S = 50S + 30S subunits; eukaryotic cytoplasmic 80S = 60S + 40S
formulas.note: S (Svedberg) units measure sedimentation rate and are not additive.

formulas.name: Size from field of view
formulas.formula: Size of one cell ≈ diameter of field of view / number of cells across it
formulas.note: Field diameter is inversely proportional to magnification.

formulas.name: Cell wall materials
formulas.formula: Plants = cellulose; Fungi = chitin; Bacteria = peptidoglycan (murein)
formulas.note: Animal cells have no cell wall.

formulas.name: Organelle functions
formulas.formula: Nucleus = control, contains DNA; Nucleolus = makes ribosomes (rRNA); Mitochondrion = aerobic respiration, ATP; Chloroplast = photosynthesis; Ribosome = protein synthesis; Lysosome = digestion, autolysis; Centriole = spindle formation in animal cells; Vacuole = storage, turgor
formulas.note: Cytoskeleton (microtubules, microfilaments) gives shape and moves organelles.

shortcuts.name: Convert to the smaller unit first
shortcuts.rule: Before dividing image by actual size, convert both to µm (multiply mm by 1000). Then the division is usually a round number.
shortcuts.example: Image 5 mm, actual 50 µm: 5 mm = 5000 µm, so M = 5000/50 = ×100.

shortcuts.name: Cube SA:V in one step
shortcuts.rule: For a cube of side L, SA:V = 6/L; no need to work out area and volume separately.
shortcuts.example: Cube of side 2 cm: 6/2 = 3:1. Side 3 cm: 6/3 = 2:1. Side 6 cm: 1:1.

shortcuts.name: Field of view scales inversely
shortcuts.rule: New field diameter = old diameter × (old magnification / new magnification).
shortcuts.example: Field is 2 mm at ×100. At ×400 it is 2 × 100/400 = 0.5 mm. If 5 cells span it, each cell ≈ 0.5/5 = 0.1 mm = 100 µm.

shortcuts.name: Plant-or-animal elimination
shortcuts.rule: Cell wall, large central vacuole or chloroplasts → plant. Centrioles or glycogen granules with no wall → animal. Mitochondria, ER, Golgi, ribosomes, nucleus → both, so they cannot decide.
shortcuts.example: 'A cell has mitochondria, centrioles and no wall' → animal cell.

shortcuts.name: The three with double membranes and DNA
shortcuts.rule: Remember 'NMC': Nucleus, Mitochondrion, Chloroplast are the only double-membrane structures, and all three hold DNA.
shortcuts.example: 'Which organelle has a double membrane but no DNA?' None of the standard ones — reject options like lysosome or Golgi, which have a single membrane.

traps: Forgetting to convert mm to µm before using M = I/A, which gives answers off by 1000.
Adding Svedberg units: 50S + 30S is 70S, not 80S.
Saying prokaryotes have no ribosomes; they have 70S ribosomes but no membrane-bound organelles.
Stating that mature red blood cells have a nucleus; mammalian RBCs lose the nucleus and mitochondria.
Calling the cell membrane fully permeable or confusing it with the freely permeable cell wall.
nsmqTips: Riddle clues such as 'suicide bag' = lysosome, 'powerhouse' = mitochondrion, 'post office' = Golgi body, 'protein factory' = ribosome, 'brain of the cell' = nucleus.
For magnification calculations, say the answer with the × sign and no units (e.g. '×400').
Have the three cell wall materials ready: cellulose, chitin, peptidoglycan — they appear as quick-fire questions.
For 'who' questions: Robert Hooke (cork cells, 1665), Leeuwenhoek (first saw living microbes), Robert Brown (nucleus), Schleiden and Schwann (cell theory), Virchow (cells from cells).

topics.summary: Substances enter and leave cells by diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion, active transport and bulk transport. NSMQ tests definitions, the effect of solutions on plant and animal cells, water potential arithmetic and factors that change diffusion rate.
keyIdeas: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration down a gradient; it is passive and needs no membrane.
Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
Facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins but is still passive (no ATP), down the gradient.
Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient using carrier proteins and ATP from respiration (e.g. mineral ion uptake by root hairs, Na⁺/K⁺ pump).
Endocytosis (phagocytosis = solids, pinocytosis = liquids) and exocytosis move bulk materials in vesicles and need ATP.
In a hypotonic solution animal cells swell and burst (haemolysis in RBCs); plant cells become turgid but do not burst because of the cell wall.
In a hypertonic solution animal cells shrink (crenation); plant cells lose water and the protoplast pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis).
Pure water has the highest water potential, 0 kPa; adding solute makes water potential negative.

formulas.name: Fick's law (proportionality)
formulas.formula: Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) / diffusion distance
formulas.note: Explains adaptations: alveoli and villi have large area, thin walls and steep gradients.

formulas.name: Water potential of a plant cell
formulas.formula: ψ = ψs + ψp
formulas.note: ψs (solute potential) is zero or negative; ψp (pressure potential) is usually positive in a turgid cell. Units kPa or MPa.

formulas.name: Direction of osmosis
formulas.formula: Water moves from higher ψ (less negative) → lower ψ (more negative)
formulas.note: −200 kPa is higher than −600 kPa.

formulas.name: Solute potential (van 't Hoff)
formulas.formula: ψs = −iCRT
formulas.note: i = ionisation constant (1 for sucrose, ≈ 2 for NaCl), C in mol m⁻³, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, T in K. 1 mol dm⁻³ sucrose at 298 K gives ψs ≈ −2.48 MPa.

formulas.name: Incipient plasmolysis
formulas.formula: At incipient plasmolysis ψp = 0, so ψ = ψs
formulas.note: Defined as the point where 50% of cells are plasmolysed; the external solution then has the same ψ as the cell sap.

formulas.name: Percentage change in mass
formulas.formula: % change = (final mass − initial mass) / initial mass × 100
formulas.note: Used in potato or yam cylinder experiments to find the isotonic concentration.

formulas.name: Graham's law (gases)
formulas.formula: Rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√M
formulas.note: M = molar mass. Lighter gases diffuse faster.

formulas.name: Tonicity terms
formulas.formula: Hypotonic = lower solute, higher ψ than cell; Isotonic = equal ψ; Hypertonic = higher solute, lower ψ than cell
formulas.note: Always state relative to the cell contents.

shortcuts.name: Water runs downhill to the more negative number
shortcuts.rule: Compare ψ values as numbers on a line: water flows toward the more negative value.
shortcuts.example: Cell A ψ = −300 kPa, cell B ψ = −500 kPa → water moves A → B, since −500 is more negative.

shortcuts.name: Add the two potentials
shortcuts.rule: ψ = ψs + ψp: just add a negative and a positive number.
shortcuts.example: ψs = −800 kPa, ψp = +300 kPa → ψ = −500 kPa.

shortcuts.name: Find the isotonic point by interpolation
shortcuts.rule: On a graph of % mass change vs concentration, the isotonic concentration is where the line crosses 0%. Between two points, zero lies at a fraction (positive value)/(positive − negative) of the way across.
shortcuts.example: +4% at 0.2 mol dm⁻³ and −2% at 0.4 mol dm⁻³: fraction = 4/6 = 2/3 of the 0.2 gap → 0.2 + 0.133 ≈ 0.33 mol dm⁻³.

shortcuts.name: Graham's law ratio by square root
shortcuts.rule: Rate A / rate B = √(M_B / M_A); pick gases whose mass ratio is a perfect square.
shortcuts.example: H₂ (2) vs O₂ (32): √(32/2) = √16 = 4, so hydrogen diffuses 4 times faster.

shortcuts.name: Multiply the Fick factors
shortcuts.rule: Each factor scales rate directly (area, gradient) or inversely (thickness); multiply the scale factors.
shortcuts.example: Double the surface area and halve the membrane thickness: rate × 2 × 2 = 4 times faster.

shortcuts.name: Plant cells never burst
shortcuts.rule: In any 'what happens' question, plant cell in water → turgid; in strong solution → plasmolysed (flaccid). Animal cell in water → bursts; in strong solution → crenated.
shortcuts.example: 'RBC placed in distilled water?' → takes in water by osmosis and bursts (haemolysis).

traps: Defining osmosis without mentioning water or the partially permeable membrane.
Calling −600 kPa a 'higher' water potential than −200 kPa; more negative is lower.
Saying facilitated diffusion uses ATP; it is passive.
Saying plant cells burst in distilled water; the cell wall prevents bursting.
Forgetting that active transport stops if respiration is inhibited (e.g. by cyanide or lack of oxygen).
nsmqTips: Expect 'Which process needs energy: diffusion, osmosis or active transport?' — answer active transport and mention ATP from respiration.
For true/false rounds, watch the word 'net': diffusion and osmosis are net movements.
If asked for the isotonic concentration from data, look for the concentration where mass change is zero; interpolate if needed.
Give everyday examples fast: wilting of salted vegetables (plasmolysis), raisins swelling in water (osmosis), scent spreading in a room (diffusion).

topics.topic: Cell division and the cell cycle
topics.summary: Cells divide by mitosis for growth, repair and asexual reproduction, and by meiosis to make haploid gametes with genetic variation. NSMQ asks for the stage in which an event happens, chromosome and DNA counts, and calculations from cell counts.
keyIdeas: The cell cycle is interphase (G1, S, G2) followed by mitosis (M phase) and cytokinesis; interphase takes most of the cycle (about 90%).
DNA replication happens in the S phase of interphase, not during prophase.

Mitosis stages: prophase (chromosomes condense, nuclear envelope breaks down, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes line up at the equator), anaphase (sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles), telophase (nuclear envelopes reform).
Mitosis gives two genetically identical diploid daughter cells; meiosis gives four genetically different haploid cells.
In prophase I of meiosis homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis, bivalents) and cross over at chiasmata.
Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (reduction division); meiosis II separates sister chromatids (like mitosis).
Variation in meiosis comes from crossing over and independent assortment of homologues in metaphase I; random fertilisation adds more.
Animal cells divide the cytoplasm by a cleavage furrow; plant cells form a cell plate from Golgi vesicles. Uncontrolled mitosis causes tumours (cancer).

formulas.name: Mitosis vs meiosis outcome
formulas.formula: Mitosis: 2n → 2 cells of 2n (identical). Meiosis: 2n → 4 cells of n (different)
formulas.note: n = haploid number; humans 2n = 46, n = 23.

formulas.name: Cell cycle sequence
formulas.formula: G1 → S → G2 → M (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) → cytokinesis
formulas.note: G0 is a resting state for cells that stop dividing (e.g. most neurons).

formulas.name: Mitotic index
formulas.formula: Mitotic index = number of cells in mitosis / total number of cells observed
formulas.note: Multiply by 100 for a percentage. A high index indicates rapid growth, e.g. root tip meristem or tumour tissue.

formulas.name: Duration of a stage
formulas.formula: Time in stage = (cells in that stage / total cells) × total cycle time
formulas.note: Assumes cells are dividing asynchronously and the sample is large.

formulas.name: Combinations from independent assortment
formulas.formula: Number of chromosome combinations in gametes = 2ⁿ
formulas.note: n = haploid number (number of homologous pairs). Ignores crossing over.

formulas.name: DNA content through the cycle
formulas.formula: G1 = 2C; after S (G2, prophase) = 4C; after meiosis I = 2C; gamete = C
formulas.note: C = DNA content of one haploid set.

formulas.name: Cells after repeated division
formulas.formula: Number of cells after k divisions = 2ᵏ (from one cell)
formulas.note: Assumes every cell divides each time.

formulas.name: Chromatid count
formulas.formula: Chromatids = 2 × chromosomes from S phase until anaphase
formulas.note: Count chromosomes by counting centromeres.

shortcuts.name: IPMAT with meanings
shortcuts.rule: Interphase, Prophase (Prepare), Metaphase (Middle), Anaphase (Apart), Telophase (Two nuclei).
shortcuts.example: 'Chromosomes align at the equator?' Middle → metaphase. 'Chromatids move to poles?' Apart → anaphase.

shortcuts.name: Fraction of cells = fraction of time
shortcuts.rule: Divide cells in the stage by total cells, then multiply by cycle time; simplify the fraction first.
shortcuts.example: 20 of 400 cells are in metaphase, cycle 24 h: 20/400 = 1/20, so 24/20 = 1.2 h = 72 min.

shortcuts.name: 2ⁿ with known powers
shortcuts.rule: Use 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≈ 10³ to estimate large powers fast.
shortcuts.example: Drosophila 2n = 8, so n = 4 and 2⁴ = 16 combinations. Humans n = 23: 2²³ = 2³ × 2²⁰ ≈ 8 × 10⁶ (exactly 8 388 608).

shortcuts.name: Count centromeres, not arms
shortcuts.rule: One centromere = one chromosome, whether it has one or two chromatids. In mitotic anaphase the chromosome number in the cell temporarily doubles.
shortcuts.example: Human cell at metaphase of mitosis: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids. At anaphase: 92 chromosomes (46 moving to each pole).

shortcuts.name: Roman numeral rule for meiosis
shortcuts.rule: Event involving homologous PAIRS (pairing, crossing over, separation of homologues) → meiosis I. Event involving sister chromatids separating → meiosis II (or mitosis).
shortcuts.example: 'Chiasmata form in?' pairs → prophase I. 'Sister chromatids separate in meiosis?' → anaphase II.

traps: Placing DNA replication in prophase instead of the S phase of interphase.
Saying crossing over occurs in prophase II; it occurs in prophase I.
Counting chromatids as chromosomes when reading diagrams.
Stating that meiosis II halves the chromosome number; the halving happens in meiosis I.
Saying plant cells form a cleavage furrow; they form a cell plate.
nsmqTips: Quick-fire questions love 'In which phase...?' — answer with the phase name and, for meiosis, the numeral (e.g. 'anaphase I').
For chromosome-count questions, state n first, then apply the rule for the stage asked.
Know sites: mitosis in root and shoot tips (meristems), bone marrow, skin; meiosis in anthers, ovules, testes and ovaries.
Colchicine stops spindle formation and halts cells at metaphase — a favourite 'name the chemical' question.

topics.summary: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids are the main molecules of life, built by condensation and broken by hydrolysis, and enzymes are protein catalysts that control the rate of these reactions. NSMQ asks for food tests, bond names, monomers and the effects of temperature, pH and inhibitors on enzymes.
keyIdeas: Monomers join by condensation (water released) and polymers are broken by hydrolysis (water added).

Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose), disaccharides (maltose = glucose + glucose, sucrose = glucose + fructose, lactose = glucose + galactose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose); bond = glycosidic bond.
Lipids: a triglyceride is glycerol + 3 fatty acids joined by ester bonds; lipids are not polymers.
Proteins are polymers of about 20 amino acids joined by peptide bonds; structure levels are primary, secondary (α-helix, β-sheet), tertiary and quaternary.
Enzymes lower the activation energy, are specific to their substrate (lock and key; induced fit) and are not used up.
Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum (about 37–40 °C for human enzymes); above it the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured. Low temperature only inactivates it.
Each enzyme has an optimum pH: pepsin ≈ 2, salivary amylase ≈ 7, pancreatic enzymes ≈ 8.
Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site; non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change the active site's shape.

formulas.name: Glucose
formulas.formula: C₆H₁₂O₆, Mr = 180
formulas.note: α-glucose forms starch and glycogen; β-glucose forms cellulose.

formulas.name: Condensation of two monosaccharides
formulas.formula: C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆ → C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O
formulas.note: Makes a disaccharide (maltose, sucrose, lactose), Mr = 342.

formulas.name: Water lost when forming a chain
formulas.formula: Joining n monomers into one chain releases (n − 1) H₂O
formulas.note: Same rule for polysaccharides and polypeptides (n − 1 peptide bonds).

formulas.name: Triglyceride formation
formulas.formula: Glycerol + 3 fatty acids → triglyceride + 3 H₂O (3 ester bonds)
formulas.note: Phospholipid: one fatty acid replaced by a phosphate group.

formulas.name: Amino acid general structure
formulas.formula: H₂N–CH(R)–COOH
formulas.note: Amino group, carboxyl group and variable R group on a central carbon. Peptide bond: –CO–NH–.

formulas.name: Energy value of food
formulas.formula: Carbohydrate ≈ 17 kJ g⁻¹; Protein ≈ 17 kJ g⁻¹; Lipid ≈ 39 kJ g⁻¹
formulas.note: Fat gives over twice the energy per gram.

formulas.name: Temperature coefficient
formulas.formula: Q₁₀ = rate at (T + 10 °C) / rate at T
formulas.note: About 2 for most enzyme reactions below the optimum.

formulas.name: Michaelis–Menten equation
formulas.formula: v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S])
formulas.note: Km = substrate concentration at which v = Vmax/2; a low Km means high affinity.

formulas.name: Rate from time
formulas.formula: Rate = 1 / time (or amount of product / time)
formulas.note: E.g. time for starch to disappear in iodine tests.

formulas.name: Food tests
formulas.formula: Starch: iodine, brown → blue-black. Reducing sugar: Benedict's + heat, blue → green/yellow/brick-red. Protein: biuret, blue → violet (purple). Lipid: ethanol emulsion → milky white; Sudan III → red layer. Vitamin C: DCPIP, blue → colourless
formulas.note: Non-reducing sugar (sucrose): boil with dilute HCl, neutralise with NaHCO₃, then Benedict's.

shortcuts.name: Mass of an oligosaccharide
shortcuts.rule: Mr = n × 180 − (n − 1) × 18 for n glucose units.
shortcuts.example: 3 glucose: 540 − 36 = 504, formula C₁₈H₃₂O₁₆ (C₁₈H₃₆O₁₈ minus 2 H₂O).

shortcuts.name: Q₁₀ as powers of 2
shortcuts.rule: For Q₁₀ = 2, each 10 °C rise below the optimum doubles the rate, so a rise of 10k °C multiplies the rate by 2ᵏ.
shortcuts.example: Rate 5 units at 15 °C. At 35 °C (two 10 °C steps): 5 × 2² = 20 units.

shortcuts.name: Michaelis–Menten fractions
shortcuts.rule: If [S] = k × Km then v = k/(k + 1) × Vmax.
shortcuts.example: [S] = Km → v = ½ Vmax. [S] = 3Km → v = ¾ Vmax. [S] = 9Km → v = 0.9 Vmax.

shortcuts.name: Inhibitor fingerprint
shortcuts.rule: Competitive: Vmax unchanged, Km increases, overcome by adding more substrate. Non-competitive: Vmax decreases, Km unchanged, not overcome by substrate.
shortcuts.example: 'Adding more substrate restores the rate' → competitive inhibitor (e.g. malonate inhibiting succinate dehydrogenase).

shortcuts.name: Reducing sugar shortcut
shortcuts.rule: All monosaccharides and the disaccharides maltose and lactose are reducing; sucrose is the classic non-reducing sugar.
shortcuts.example: 'Which gives a negative Benedict's test: glucose, maltose, sucrose, lactose?' → sucrose.

shortcuts.name: Disaccharide pairs mnemonic
shortcuts.rule: 'Mal-Glu-Glu, Sue-Glu-Fru, Lac-Glu-Gal': maltose = glucose + glucose, sucrose = glucose + fructose, lactose = glucose + galactose.
shortcuts.example: 'Hydrolysis of lactose gives?' → glucose and galactose.

traps: Saying enzymes are 'killed' at high temperature; they are denatured (not alive).
Saying low temperature denatures enzymes; it only slows molecular movement.
Forgetting to heat Benedict's test, or using Benedict's on sucrose without hydrolysing first.
Calling lipids polymers; triglycerides are not made of repeating monomers.
Thinking enzymes are used up or change the end position of equilibrium; they only speed up reaching it.
nsmqTips: Food test questions are usually 'reagent → colour'; answer with the final positive colour.
Name the bond quickly: glycosidic (carbohydrates), ester (lipids), peptide (proteins), phosphodiester (nucleic acids).
For graph-reading rounds, the optimum is the peak; the steep fall after it is denaturation.
Cofactor examples: Cl⁻ for salivary amylase, Zn²⁺ for carbonic anhydrase; coenzymes such as NAD and FAD come from B vitamins.

topics.summary: Molecular biology covers DNA structure, replication, transcription, translation and gene regulation; biotechnology uses these tools (restriction enzymes, PCR, cloning, gel electrophoresis, sequencing, CRISPR) to study and change organisms. NSMQ and first-year university questions test base-pairing calculations, the genetic code and how lab techniques work.
keyIdeas: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands (5'→3' and 3'→5') held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: A with T (2 H-bonds), G with C (3 H-bonds).
A and G are purines (two rings); C, T and U are pyrimidines (one ring). RNA uses ribose and uracil instead of deoxyribose and thymine.
Replication is semi-conservative (Meselson–Stahl): helicase unwinds, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the 5'→3' direction, the lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments joined by ligase.
Central dogma: DNA → (transcription by RNA polymerase) → mRNA → (translation on ribosomes) → protein; retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to make DNA from RNA.
The genetic code is a triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate and nearly universal code; AUG (methionine) starts translation; UAA, UAG, UGA stop it.
Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed: 5' cap, poly-A tail and splicing out of introns; exons are kept.
Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences, often leaving sticky ends; DNA ligase joins fragments to make recombinant DNA, carried into cells by vectors (plasmids, viruses).
In gel electrophoresis DNA (negative because of phosphate) moves toward the anode (+), and shorter fragments travel farther.

formulas.name: Chargaff's rules (double-stranded DNA)
formulas.note: Purines equal pyrimidines. Does not apply to single-stranded RNA or DNA.

formulas.name: Finding the other bases
formulas.note: Given any one base percentage in dsDNA.

formulas.name: Hydrogen bonds in a duplex
formulas.formula: Total H-bonds = 2 × (A–T pairs) + 3 × (G–C pairs)
formulas.note: More G–C content means higher melting temperature.

formulas.name: Number of codons
formulas.formula: 4³ = 64 codons: 61 code for amino acids, 3 are stop codons
formulas.note: A doublet code would give only 4² = 16, too few for 20 amino acids.

formulas.name: Coding length of a gene
formulas.formula: Coding nucleotides = 3 × (number of amino acids) + 3 (stop codon)
formulas.note: Excludes introns and untranslated regions.

formulas.name: B-DNA dimensions
formulas.formula: 0.34 nm per base pair; ≈ 10 bp per turn; ≈ 3.4 nm per turn; diameter ≈ 2 nm
formulas.note: So 1 kb of DNA is about 340 nm long.

formulas.name: PCR amplification
formulas.formula: Copies after n cycles = N₀ × 2ⁿ (ideal)
formulas.note: Each cycle: denature ≈ 94–95 °C, anneal primers ≈ 50–65 °C, extend ≈ 72 °C with heat-stable Taq polymerase.

formulas.name: Primer melting temperature (Wallace rule)
formulas.note: Rough estimate for short oligonucleotides (about 14–20 nucleotides).

formulas.name: Expected restriction site spacing
formulas.formula: A site of n specific bases occurs on average once every 4ⁿ bp
formulas.note: Assumes random sequence with equal base frequencies.

formulas.name: Codon–anticodon pairing
formulas.formula: DNA template 3'-TAC-5' → mRNA 5'-AUG-3' → tRNA anticodon 3'-UAC-5'
formulas.note: The mRNA matches the coding (sense) strand with U in place of T.

shortcuts.name: Chargaff in one line
shortcuts.rule: Double the given base, subtract from 100, halve what is left for each of the other pair.

shortcuts.name: H-bond count from base composition
shortcuts.rule: In N bp of dsDNA, %A + %T of the bases equals the percentage of A–T pairs.
shortcuts.example: 100 bp with A = 30%: A + T = 60% → 60 A–T pairs and 40 G–C pairs. H-bonds = 2×60 + 3×40 = 120 + 120 = 240.

shortcuts.name: PCR with 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³
shortcuts.rule: Break the number of cycles into tens: every 10 cycles multiplies by about 1000.
shortcuts.example: One template, 30 cycles: 2³⁰ = (2¹⁰)³ ≈ (10³)³ = 10⁹ copies (exactly 1 073 741 824).

shortcuts.name: Wallace rule mentally
shortcuts.rule: Count A+T and G+C in the primer, multiply by 2 and 4, add.

shortcuts.name: Cutter frequency powers of 4
shortcuts.rule: 4⁴ = 256, 4⁶ = 4096, 4⁸ = 65 536: four-, six- and eight-base cutters.
shortcuts.example: EcoRI recognises 6 bp (GAATTC): expect a cut about every 4096 bp, so a 40 960 bp random DNA gives about 10 cuts.

shortcuts.name: Write complements reversed
shortcuts.rule: To write the complementary strand 5'→3', complement each base and read the result backwards.
shortcuts.example: 5'-ATGCCG-3' → complement 3'-TACGGC-5' → written 5'→3' as 5'-GCCGTA-3'.

traps: Applying Chargaff's rules to single-stranded RNA.
Writing T in mRNA or forgetting that the strands are antiparallel when writing complements.
Saying DNA moves to the cathode in electrophoresis; it moves to the anode (+).
Thinking the gene length equals 3 × amino acids exactly; add the stop codon, and remember introns in eukaryotic genes.
Confusing transcription (nucleus, makes RNA) with translation (ribosome, makes protein).
nsmqTips: Base percentage questions take under 10 s with the 'double, subtract, halve' rule — say all four values.

Know the 'who': Watson and Crick (structure, 1953, using Franklin and Wilkins' X-ray data), Meselson and Stahl (semi-conservative replication), Kary Mullis (PCR), Doudna and Charpentier (CRISPR–Cas9).
If asked why Taq polymerase is used, answer: it is heat-stable, from Thermus aquaticus, so it survives the 95 °C denaturation step.
Applications to mention: insulin from recombinant bacteria, Bt crops, DNA fingerprinting in forensics and paternity, gene therapy, PCR-based diagnosis (e.g. COVID-19 tests).

topics.summary: Green plants are autotrophs that use light energy, captured by chlorophyll, to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. NSMQ asks for the equation, the two stages and where they happen, limiting factors, leaf adaptations and classic experiments.
keyIdeas: Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts: light-dependent reactions on the thylakoid membranes (grana), light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) in the stroma.
Light-dependent stage: light excites chlorophyll, water is split (photolysis) releasing O₂, and ATP and NADPH (reduced NADP) are made.

Light-independent stage: CO₂ combines with ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP, 5C) using the enzyme rubisco to give two molecules of glycerate-3-phosphate (GP, 3C), which are reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and NADPH.
All the oxygen released comes from water, not carbon dioxide (shown with ¹⁸O isotope labelling).
Chlorophyll absorbs mainly blue and red light and reflects green light.
Limiting factors are light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature; the rate is set by whichever is in shortest supply.
Leaf adaptations: large flat surface, thin, palisade cells packed with chloroplasts near the top, air spaces in spongy mesophyll, stomata for gas exchange, veins for transport.
C₄ plants (maize, sugarcane) fix CO₂ first with PEP carboxylase into a 4C compound; CAM plants (pineapple, cacti) open stomata at night to save water.

formulas.name: Overall equation
formulas.formula: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (light energy, chlorophyll)
formulas.note: Fuller version showing the true O₂ source: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O.

formulas.name: Photolysis of water
formulas.formula: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂
formulas.note: Occurs at photosystem II; the electrons replace those lost by chlorophyll.

formulas.name: Carbon fixation
formulas.formula: CO₂ + RuBP (5C) → 2 GP (3C), catalysed by rubisco
formulas.note: GP is also called PGA (3-phosphoglycerate).

formulas.name: Energy cost per CO₂ fixed
formulas.formula: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂
formulas.note: So one glucose (6 CO₂, six turns of the cycle) costs 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

formulas.name: Photosystems
formulas.formula: PSII reaction centre P680; PSI reaction centre P700
formulas.note: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation uses both and makes ATP, NADPH and O₂; cyclic uses only PSI and makes ATP only.

formulas.name: Rf value (chromatography)
formulas.formula: Rf = distance moved by pigment / distance moved by solvent front
formulas.note: Always less than 1. Carotene runs highest; chlorophyll b runs lowest of the main pigments.

formulas.name: Light intensity and distance
formulas.formula: Light intensity ∝ 1/d²
formulas.note: Used in pondweed bubble experiments with a lamp at different distances.

formulas.name: Absorption peaks
formulas.formula: Chlorophyll absorbs blue (≈ 430–450 nm) and red (≈ 640–680 nm); reflects green (≈ 500–560 nm)
formulas.note: An action spectrum shows the rate at each wavelength and closely matches the absorption spectrum.

formulas.name: Starch test on a leaf
formulas.formula: Boil in water → boil in ethanol (water bath) → rinse in warm water → iodine: blue-black where starch is present
formulas.note: Destarch the plant first by keeping it in the dark for 24–48 h.

shortcuts.name: Calvin cycle tally by sixes
shortcuts.rule: Per CO₂: 3 ATP, 2 NADPH. Multiply by the number of CO₂ fixed.
shortcuts.example: One glucose = 6 CO₂: 6 × 3 = 18 ATP and 6 × 2 = 12 NADPH. One exported triose phosphate = 3 CO₂: 9 ATP, 6 NADPH.

shortcuts.name: Inverse square for lamp distance
shortcuts.rule: Double the distance → intensity ÷ 4; triple → ÷ 9; halve → × 4.
shortcuts.example: Lamp moved from 10 cm to 20 cm: intensity becomes ¼. Moved from 30 cm to 10 cm: intensity × 9.

shortcuts.name: Follow the labelled atom
shortcuts.rule: O in O₂ comes from water; O in glucose and the new water comes from CO₂; C in glucose comes from CO₂.
shortcuts.example: Plant given H₂¹⁸O → labelled O₂ released. Plant given C¹⁸O₂ → label appears in glucose (and water), not in O₂.

shortcuts.name: Rf as a fraction
shortcuts.rule: Simplify the two distances as a fraction before converting to a decimal.
shortcuts.example: Pigment 3.6 cm, solvent front 6.0 cm: 36/60 = 3/5 = 0.6.

shortcuts.name: Which factor is limiting
shortcuts.rule: On a rate graph, if increasing a factor raises the rate, that factor is limiting; once the line levels off, something else is limiting.
shortcuts.example: Rate stops rising with light at 0.04% CO₂ but rises again at 0.1% CO₂ → on the plateau, CO₂ was the limiting factor.

shortcuts.name: Mnemonic for the two stages
shortcuts.rule: 'Thylakoid = Light, Stroma = Sugar': light-dependent in thylakoids, sugar-making Calvin cycle in stroma.
shortcuts.example: 'Where is rubisco found?' Sugar-making → stroma.

traps: Saying the oxygen comes from carbon dioxide; it comes from water.
Calling the light-independent stage a 'dark reaction' that happens only at night; it runs in light, using ATP and NADPH from the light stage.
Writing NAD instead of NADP for photosynthesis.
Saying plants photosynthesise instead of respiring; plants respire all the time, day and night.
Saying chlorophyll absorbs green light; it reflects green.
nsmqTips: When asked for the equation, give the balanced 6CO₂ + 6H₂O form and say 'in the presence of light and chlorophyll'.

Classic experiments: Van Helmont (willow tree: its gain in mass did not come from the soil), Priestley (plant restores air), Ingenhousz (light needed), Engelmann (bacteria and spectrum), Calvin (¹⁴C and the cycle).
Compensation point: light intensity at which photosynthesis rate equals respiration rate, so net gas exchange is zero.
Mineral roles: Mg²⁺ is part of chlorophyll (deficiency → chlorosis), nitrate for amino acids, phosphate for ATP and nucleic acids.

topics.summary: Animals are heterotrophs that ingest, digest, absorb, assimilate and egest food, using enzymes along the alimentary canal to break large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones. NSMQ asks for enzyme–substrate–product sets, sites and pH of digestion, dental formulae, deficiency diseases and food energy calculations.
keyIdeas: Five stages: ingestion, digestion (mechanical and chemical), absorption, assimilation, egestion.
Starch digestion starts in the mouth (salivary amylase), protein digestion starts in the stomach (pepsin), fat digestion happens mainly in the duodenum and ileum (lipase after bile emulsification).
The stomach secretes HCl (pH ≈ 1.5–2), which kills microbes and activates pepsinogen to pepsin; rennin clots milk protein in young mammals.
Bile is made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder, contains no enzymes, emulsifies fats and neutralises acid chyme.
The pancreas secretes amylase, trypsin(ogen) and lipase in an alkaline juice with hydrogencarbonate.
The ileum absorbs digested food through villi and microvilli; glucose and amino acids go into blood capillaries to the hepatic portal vein, fatty acids and glycerol into lacteals (lymph).
The colon absorbs water and minerals; undigested material is egested as faeces.
A balanced diet has carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and fibre (roughage) in the right proportions.

formulas.name: Enzymes in the mouth and stomach
formulas.formula: Salivary amylase: starch → maltose (mouth, pH ≈ 7). Pepsin: proteins → polypeptides (stomach, pH ≈ 2). Rennin: caseinogen → casein (clots milk)
formulas.note: Pepsin is secreted as inactive pepsinogen, activated by HCl.

formulas.name: Enzymes in the small intestine
formulas.formula: Pancreatic amylase: starch → maltose. Trypsin: proteins → polypeptides. Lipase: fats → fatty acids + glycerol. Maltase: maltose → glucose. Sucrase: sucrose → glucose + fructose. Lactase: lactose → glucose + galactose. Peptidases: peptides → amino acids
formulas.note: Trypsinogen is activated by enterokinase (enteropeptidase) from the duodenal wall.

formulas.name: Energy value of a food (calorimetry)
formulas.formula: Energy per gram = (mass of water × 4.2 × ΔT) / mass of food burned
formulas.note: Specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Result in J g⁻¹; usually underestimates because of heat loss.

formulas.name: Body mass index
formulas.formula: BMI = mass (kg) / height² (m²)
formulas.note: 18.5–24.9 is the normal range for adults.

formulas.name: Human dental formula
formulas.formula: Adult: I 2/2, C 1/1, PM 2/2, M 3/3 = 32 teeth. Milk teeth: I 2/2, C 1/1, M 2/2 = 20
formulas.note: Numbers are for one side; upper over lower jaw.

formulas.name: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies
formulas.formula: A: night blindness, xerophthalmia. D: rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults). E: reproductive problems, anaemia. K: poor blood clotting
formulas.note: Vitamin D is made in skin exposed to sunlight.

formulas.name: Water-soluble vitamin deficiencies
formulas.formula: B₁ (thiamine): beriberi. B₃ (niacin): pellagra. B₁₂ / folic acid: anaemia. C (ascorbic acid): scurvy
formulas.note: Water-soluble vitamins are not stored and are lost in cooking water.

formulas.name: Mineral and protein deficiencies
formulas.formula: Iron: anaemia. Iodine: goitre. Calcium: rickets, weak teeth. Protein: kwashiorkor. Protein and energy: marasmus
formulas.note: Kwashiorkor shows oedema (swollen belly), discoloured hair; marasmus shows extreme wasting.

shortcuts.name: Dental formula total in one step
shortcuts.rule: Total teeth = 2 × (sum of all numbers in the formula).

shortcuts.name: Calorimetry with round numbers
shortcuts.rule: Multiply water mass × ΔT first, then × 4.2.
shortcuts.example: 1 g of groundnut heats 20 g of water by 25 °C: 20 × 25 = 500, × 4.2 = 2100 J, so 2.1 kJ g⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Enzyme name tells the substrate
shortcuts.rule: Drop -ase to get the substrate: maltase → maltose, lactase → lactose, lipase → lipid, protease → protein. '-ogen' = inactive form.
shortcuts.example: 'What does sucrase act on and produce?' sucrose → glucose + fructose.

shortcuts.name: pH journey mnemonic
shortcuts.rule: 'Neutral, Acid, Alkaline': mouth ≈ 7, stomach ≈ 2, duodenum/ileum ≈ 8.
shortcuts.example: 'Why does salivary amylase stop working in the stomach?' The pH drops to about 2, so it is denatured.

shortcuts.name: Vitamin mnemonic ADEK
shortcuts.rule: Fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, K ('A DEcK of fats'); all others in the syllabus (B group, C) are water-soluble.
shortcuts.example: 'Which vitamin is fat-soluble: B₁, C or K?' → K.

traps: Saying bile contains enzymes or digests fat; it only emulsifies.
Saying trypsin is made in the stomach; it is made by the pancreas and works in the duodenum.
Placing the start of protein digestion in the mouth.
Saying the large intestine absorbs digested food; it mainly absorbs water.
Confusing kwashiorkor (protein deficiency) with marasmus (protein and energy deficiency).
nsmqTips: Enzyme questions usually need three parts: enzyme, substrate, product. Say all three quickly.
Remember that fatty acids and glycerol go into the lacteals, not directly into blood capillaries.
Teeth types and jobs: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind; herbivores have a diastema (gap).
Know special nutrition modes: saprophytic (fungi), parasitic (tapeworm, dodder), holozoic (humans), symbiotic (Rhizobium in legume nodules).

topics.summary: Respiration is the release of energy from food (mainly glucose) in all living cells, producing ATP. NSMQ asks for aerobic and anaerobic equations, the stages and their locations, ATP yields, respiratory quotients and respirometer calculations.
keyIdeas: Respiration is a chemical process in cells; breathing (ventilation) is the mechanical movement of air in and out of the lungs.
Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm: glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (3C), net 2 ATP and 2 NADH; it needs no oxygen.

The link reaction (pyruvate → acetyl CoA + CO₂) and the Krebs cycle occur in the mitochondrial matrix; oxidative phosphorylation occurs on the inner membrane (cristae) via the electron transport chain.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, combining with electrons and H⁺ to form water.
Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces lactic acid; in yeast and plants it produces ethanol and CO₂ (alcoholic fermentation).
After vigorous exercise, the oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed to oxidise accumulated lactic acid.
Uses of energy: muscle contraction, active transport, protein synthesis, cell division, nerve impulses, maintaining body temperature.

formulas.name: Aerobic respiration
formulas.formula: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (≈ 2880 kJ per mole of glucose)
formulas.note: Part of the energy is trapped as ATP; the rest is lost as heat.

formulas.name: Anaerobic respiration in animals
formulas.formula: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ (lactic acid) + energy (2 ATP)
formulas.note: No CO₂ is produced.

formulas.name: Alcoholic fermentation (yeast, plants)
formulas.formula: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy (2 ATP)
formulas.note: Basis of brewing (ethanol) and baking (CO₂ makes dough rise).

formulas.name: Respiratory quotient
formulas.formula: RQ = volume of CO₂ produced / volume of O₂ consumed
formulas.note: Carbohydrate = 1.0, protein ≈ 0.9, lipid ≈ 0.7. RQ > 1 suggests some anaerobic respiration.

formulas.name: Glycolysis summary
formulas.formula: Glucose + 2 NAD + 2 ADP + 2 Pi → 2 pyruvate + 2 NADH + 2 ATP (net)
formulas.note: 4 ATP made, 2 used in the investment phase.

formulas.name: Link reaction and Krebs per glucose
formulas.formula: Link: 2 CO₂, 2 NADH. Krebs (2 turns): 4 CO₂, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP
formulas.note: Total CO₂ per glucose = 6.

formulas.name: ATP per reduced coenzyme
formulas.formula: Modern: NADH ≈ 2.5 ATP, FADH₂ ≈ 1.5 ATP. Older textbooks: NADH = 3, FADH₂ = 2
formulas.note: Gives ≈ 30–32 ATP per glucose (modern) or 36–38 (older figure).

formulas.name: Respirometer gas volume
formulas.formula: Volume = πr² × distance moved by the liquid
formulas.note: r = internal radius of the capillary. KOH or soda lime absorbs CO₂, so the movement measures O₂ uptake.

shortcuts.name: RQ by recognition
shortcuts.rule: Do not calculate if the number is standard: ≈ 1.0 carbohydrate, ≈ 0.9 protein, ≈ 0.7 fat, above 1 = anaerobic contribution, 0 = no CO₂ (e.g. lactic acid fermentation).
shortcuts.example: Seeds give RQ = 0.71 → they are respiring lipid (oily seeds such as groundnut).

shortcuts.name: Glucose RQ from the equation
shortcuts.rule: For any balanced equation, RQ = coefficient of CO₂ / coefficient of O₂.
shortcuts.example: Glucose: 6 CO₂ / 6 O₂ = 1. Tripalmitin: 2C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O, RQ = 102/145 ≈ 0.70.

shortcuts.name: ATP tally
shortcuts.rule: Count 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂ per glucose plus 4 ATP made directly (2 glycolysis + 2 Krebs).

shortcuts.name: Respirometer with r² first
shortcuts.rule: Square the radius (not the diameter), then multiply by distance and π ≈ 3.14.
shortcuts.example: Capillary diameter 1 mm (r = 0.5 mm), liquid moves 25 mm: 0.25 × 25 = 6.25, × π ≈ 19.6 mm³ of O₂.

shortcuts.name: Where does each stage happen
shortcuts.rule: 'Glyco in the Cyto; Link and Krebs in the Matrix; Chain on the Cristae'.
shortcuts.example: 'Where is the electron transport chain?' → inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae).

traps: Using 'respiration' and 'breathing' as the same thing.
Saying anaerobic respiration in human muscle produces CO₂.
Placing glycolysis in the mitochondria; it occurs in the cytoplasm.
Saying plants respire only at night; they respire all the time.
Forgetting that the respirometer must be kept at constant temperature and needs a control with dead (boiled) material or glass beads.
nsmqTips: When asked for the products of anaerobic respiration, say which organism: lactic acid for animals, ethanol and CO₂ for yeast and plants.
Have the energy figure ready: about 2880 kJ per mole of glucose aerobically, against only 2 ATP net anaerobically.
If asked what limewater shows: it turns milky with CO₂; hydrogencarbonate indicator turns from red to yellow when CO₂ rises.
Name the final electron acceptor (oxygen) and the poison that blocks the chain (cyanide) — common quick-fire questions.

topics.summary: Gaseous exchange is the diffusion of oxygen into and carbon dioxide out of an organism across a respiratory surface, while breathing is the movement of air or water over that surface. NSMQ asks about breathing mechanics, lung volumes, composition of inhaled and exhaled air and gas exchange surfaces in different organisms.
keyIdeas: Good respiratory surfaces are large, thin (short diffusion distance), moist, well supplied with blood and well ventilated, keeping a steep gradient.
In humans air passes nostrils → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli; cartilage rings keep the trachea open.
Inspiration: external intercostal muscles contract (ribs move up and out) and the diaphragm contracts and flattens; thoracic volume rises, pressure falls, air rushes in.
Quiet expiration is mostly passive: muscles relax, elastic lungs recoil, volume falls, pressure rises, air is pushed out; forced expiration uses internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.
Breathing rate is controlled by the medulla oblongata, which responds mainly to a rise in blood CO₂ (fall in pH).

Fish use gills with a countercurrent flow of blood and water; insects use spiracles and tracheae carrying air straight to tissues; frogs use skin, mouth lining and lungs; plants use stomata and lenticels.
Smoking: tar damages cilia and causes cancer, carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin, nicotine is addictive and raises blood pressure; emphysema reduces alveolar surface area.

formulas.name: Pulmonary ventilation rate
formulas.formula: Ventilation rate = tidal volume × breathing rate
formulas.note: At rest ≈ 0.5 dm³ × 12 min⁻¹ = 6 dm³ min⁻¹.

formulas.name: Alveolar ventilation
formulas.formula: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space volume) × breathing rate
formulas.note: Anatomical dead space ≈ 150 cm³ (air in trachea and bronchi that does not reach alveoli).

formulas.name: Lung volumes
formulas.formula: Vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume; Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume
formulas.note: Typical adult: tidal ≈ 0.5 dm³, vital capacity ≈ 4–5 dm³, residual ≈ 1–1.5 dm³.

formulas.name: Boyle's law (basis of breathing)
formulas.formula: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (constant temperature)
formulas.note: Increasing chest volume lowers pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in.

formulas.name: Composition of inhaled and exhaled air
formulas.formula: Inhaled: O₂ ≈ 21%, CO₂ ≈ 0.04%, N₂ ≈ 78%. Exhaled: O₂ ≈ 16%, CO₂ ≈ 4%, N₂ ≈ 78%, saturated with water vapour
formulas.note: Exhaled air is also warmer.

formulas.name: Fick's law at the alveolus
formulas.formula: Rate ∝ surface area × (partial pressure difference) / wall thickness
formulas.note: Alveolar wall plus capillary wall is about 0.5 µm thick; total alveolar area ≈ 70 m².

formulas.name: Respiratory surfaces by organism
formulas.formula: Mammals, birds, reptiles: lungs. Fish: gills. Insects: tracheae via spiracles. Earthworm: moist skin. Amoeba: cell membrane. Frog: skin, buccal cavity, lungs. Plants: stomata, lenticels
formulas.note: Birds have air sacs and one-way airflow through parabronchi.

formulas.name: Breathing rate from a spirometer trace
formulas.formula: Breaths per minute = number of peaks / time in seconds × 60
formulas.note: Tidal volume = height of one peak-to-trough; the trace slopes downward as CO₂ is absorbed and O₂ used.

shortcuts.name: Ventilation in cm³ then convert
shortcuts.rule: Multiply tidal volume in cm³ by rate, then divide by 1000 for dm³.
shortcuts.example: Tidal volume 500 cm³, rate 15 min⁻¹: 7500 cm³ min⁻¹ = 7.5 dm³ min⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Subtract dead space first
shortcuts.rule: Alveolar ventilation: take 150 cm³ off the tidal volume, then multiply.
shortcuts.example: Tidal 500 cm³, dead space 150 cm³, rate 12: 350 × 12 = 4200 cm³ min⁻¹ = 4.2 dm³ min⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Scale the trace to one minute
shortcuts.rule: Find what multiplies the time shown to 60 s and apply it to the peak count.
shortcuts.example: 6 breaths in 20 s: 60/20 = 3, so 6 × 3 = 18 breaths min⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: 'In = Contract' rule
shortcuts.rule: On inspiration both the diaphragm and external intercostals contract; on quiet expiration both relax. Contract → volume up → pressure down → air in.
shortcuts.example: 'What happens to the diaphragm during inhalation?' Contracts and flattens (moves down).

shortcuts.name: Countercurrent wins
shortcuts.rule: Countercurrent flow keeps a gradient along the whole gill, so blood can approach the O₂ level of incoming water; parallel flow reaches equilibrium at about half-way at best.
shortcuts.example: If water enters at 100% saturation, parallel flow gives blood at most about 50%; countercurrent can load to about 80–90%.

traps: Saying the diaphragm moves up during inspiration; it contracts, flattens and moves down.
Saying exhaled air contains no oxygen; it still has about 16%.
Saying the respiratory centre responds mainly to low O₂; it responds mainly to rising CO₂.
Confusing gaseous exchange (diffusion at a surface) with respiration (energy release in cells).
Forgetting dead space when working out alveolar ventilation.
nsmqTips: Give the full chain of events for breathing in one sentence: muscles contract → volume increases → pressure decreases → air enters.
Quick-fire favourites: epiglottis prevents food entering the trachea; surfactant prevents alveoli collapsing; lenticels are pores in woody stems.
When asked for the respiratory organ of an animal, think of its habitat and body size: small moist animals use skin, insects use tracheae.
Limewater experiment: exhaled air turns it milky faster than inhaled air, showing more CO₂.

topics.summary: Mammals have a closed double circulation pumped by a four-chambered heart, with blood carrying oxygen, nutrients, wastes, hormones and defence cells. NSMQ asks for the route of blood, heart structure, blood components, blood groups and cardiac output calculations.
keyIdeas: Double circulation: the pulmonary circuit (heart → lungs → heart) and the systemic circuit (heart → body → heart); blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit.
The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood to the whole body at high pressure.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick muscular elastic walls, narrow lumen, high pressure); veins return blood (thin walls, wide lumen, valves); capillaries are one cell thick for exchange.
Blood = plasma (≈ 55%) + red cells, white cells and platelets (≈ 45%).
Red blood cells are biconcave, have no nucleus and carry O₂ as oxyhaemoglobin; white cells defend (phagocytes engulf, lymphocytes make antibodies); platelets help clotting.
The heartbeat is myogenic: started by the sinoatrial node (pacemaker), passed to the atrioventricular node, then along the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres.
ABO blood groups depend on antigens on red cells and antibodies in plasma; O is the universal donor, AB the universal recipient.
Lymph returns tissue fluid to the blood through the lymphatic system; lymph nodes filter it and contain lymphocytes.

formulas.name: Cardiac output
formulas.formula: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate
formulas.note: At rest ≈ 70 cm³ × 72 min⁻¹ ≈ 5 dm³ min⁻¹.

formulas.name: Heart rate from cycle time
formulas.formula: Heart rate (beats min⁻¹) = 60 / duration of one cardiac cycle (s)
formulas.note: One cycle at rest ≈ 0.8 s → 75 beats min⁻¹.

formulas.name: Route of blood through the heart
formulas.formula: Vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral) valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta
formulas.note: Semilunar valves sit at the bases of the pulmonary artery and aorta.

formulas.name: ABO system
formulas.formula: A: antigen A, anti-B. B: antigen B, anti-A. AB: antigens A and B, no antibodies. O: no antigens, anti-A and anti-B
formulas.note: Agglutination happens when donor antigens meet recipient antibodies.

formulas.name: Blood clotting cascade
formulas.formula: Damaged tissue/platelets release thromboplastin → prothrombin → thrombin (needs Ca²⁺, vitamin K) → fibrinogen → fibrin threads trap cells
formulas.note: Haemophilia is a sex-linked failure of a clotting factor.

formulas.name: Typical blood counts
formulas.formula: Red cells ≈ 4.5–5.5 × 10¹² L⁻¹ (≈ 5 million mm⁻³); white cells ≈ 4–11 × 10⁹ L⁻¹; platelets ≈ 150–400 × 10⁹ L⁻¹
formulas.note: Red cells live about 120 days and are destroyed in the liver and spleen.

formulas.name: Haemoglobin oxygen binding
formulas.formula: Hb + 4O₂ ⇌ HbO₈ (oxyhaemoglobin); ≈ 1.34 cm³ O₂ per g of Hb when fully saturated
formulas.note: Each Hb has four haem groups, each with one Fe²⁺.

formulas.name: Blood pressure
formulas.formula: Normal adult ≈ 120/80 mmHg (systolic/diastolic)
formulas.note: Systolic = ventricles contracting; diastolic = heart relaxing.

formulas.name: Heart sounds
formulas.formula: 'Lub' = atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves closing; 'dub' = semilunar valves closing
formulas.note: Lub marks the start of ventricular systole.

shortcuts.name: Heart rate by division into 60
shortcuts.rule: Divide 60 by the R–R interval or cycle time in seconds; know 0.75 → 80, 0.8 → 75, 0.6 → 100, 1.0 → 60.
shortcuts.example: ECG peaks 0.75 s apart: 60 / 0.75 = 80 beats min⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Cardiac output rounding
shortcuts.rule: Multiply stroke volume by heart rate and convert cm³ to dm³.
shortcuts.example: 70 cm³ × 72 = 5040 cm³ ≈ 5.0 dm³ min⁻¹. During exercise, 120 cm³ × 150 = 18 000 cm³ = 18 dm³ min⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: 'Arteries Away' with the two exceptions
shortcuts.rule: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and usually oxygenated blood; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated and the pulmonary vein oxygenated blood.
shortcuts.example: 'Which artery carries deoxygenated blood?' → pulmonary artery.

shortcuts.name: LAB RAT valves
shortcuts.rule: Left Atrium → Bicuspid; Right Atrium → Tricuspid.
shortcuts.example: 'Valve between left atrium and left ventricle?' → bicuspid (mitral).

shortcuts.name: Transfusion check: donor antigen vs recipient antibody
shortcuts.rule: A transfusion is safe if the recipient's plasma has no antibody against the donor's red-cell antigen. Recipient X can receive X and O.
shortcuts.example: Recipient group B has anti-A: can receive B or O; not A or AB.

shortcuts.name: Bohr shift mnemonic 'CADET, face Right'
shortcuts.rule: More CO₂, Acid, 2,3-DPG, Exercise or Temperature shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so Hb releases O₂ more easily.
shortcuts.example: 'In active muscle, which way does the curve shift?' → right, more O₂ unloaded.

traps: Saying all arteries carry oxygenated blood.
Mixing up where antigens (on red cell surface) and antibodies (in plasma) are found.
Saying the right ventricle has the thickest wall.
Saying the hepatic portal vein goes from the liver to the heart; it carries blood from the gut to the liver.
Confusing serum (plasma without clotting factors) with plasma.
nsmqTips: For 'trace the path' questions, name chambers and valves in order without skipping the valves.
Who: William Harvey described blood circulation; Karl Landsteiner discovered ABO blood groups.
Rhesus: a Rh⁻ mother with a Rh⁺ fetus risks haemolytic disease of the newborn in later pregnancies.
Fish have a single circulation and a two-chambered heart; amphibians three chambers; mammals and birds four.

topics.summary: Plants move water and minerals upward in the xylem and sugars both ways in the phloem, with transpiration driving most water movement. NSMQ asks for the structure and function of xylem and phloem, the cohesion–tension mechanism, factors affecting transpiration, stomatal opening and potometer and ringing experiments.
keyIdeas: Xylem carries water and mineral ions from roots to leaves, in one direction only; its vessels and tracheids are dead, hollow and strengthened with lignin.
Phloem carries organic solutes (mainly sucrose, also amino acids) from sources to sinks, up or down (translocation); sieve tubes are living, with sieve plates and companion cells.

Water enters root hairs by osmosis, crosses the cortex by the apoplast (cell walls), symplast (cytoplasm via plasmodesmata) and vacuolar pathways, and the Casparian strip (suberin) in the endodermis forces it into the symplast.
Cohesion–tension theory: evaporation from leaves creates tension; cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls pull a continuous column up the plant.
Root pressure (from active pumping of ions into the xylem) and capillarity help but cannot lift water to the top of tall trees.
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves, mostly through stomata; it cools the plant and moves minerals.
Stomata open when K⁺ ions enter guard cells, lowering their water potential; water enters, the guard cells become turgid and bow apart because of their unevenly thickened walls.
Mass flow hypothesis (Münch): sugar loaded at the source lowers water potential, water enters, pressure builds and pushes sap toward the sink.

formulas.name: Xylem vs phloem
formulas.formula: Xylem: water + minerals, upward, dead lignified cells, no end walls (vessels). Phloem: sucrose + amino acids, both directions, living sieve tubes with sieve plates and companion cells
formulas.note: Both are found together in vascular bundles.

formulas.name: Potometer rate of water uptake
formulas.formula: Rate = (πr² × distance moved by bubble) / time
formulas.note: r = capillary radius. A potometer measures water uptake, which is close to but not equal to transpiration.

formulas.name: Factors affecting transpiration
formulas.formula: Rate increases with: light intensity, temperature, wind speed; rate decreases with: humidity
formulas.note: Light acts mainly by opening stomata; wind removes the humid layer next to the leaf.

formulas.name: Water potential gradient across the plant
formulas.formula: ψ soil > ψ root > ψ stem xylem > ψ leaf > ψ air
formulas.note: Water always moves to the more negative water potential.

formulas.name: Capillary rise
formulas.formula: h = 2γ cos θ / (ρ g r)
formulas.note: γ = surface tension (≈ 0.072 N m⁻¹ for water), θ = contact angle, ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, r = tube radius. Narrow tubes give higher rise.

formulas.name: Stomatal opening sequence
formulas.formula: Light → K⁺ pumped into guard cells (ATP) → ψ of guard cells falls → water enters by osmosis → guard cells turgid → pore opens
formulas.note: Closing reverses it; abscisic acid (ABA) triggers closure under water stress.

formulas.name: Root pathways
formulas.formula: Apoplast = through cell walls; Symplast = through cytoplasm and plasmodesmata; Vacuolar = through vacuoles
formulas.note: The Casparian strip blocks the apoplast at the endodermis, letting the plant control mineral entry.

formulas.name: Xerophyte adaptations
formulas.formula: Thick waxy cuticle, sunken stomata, rolled leaves, hairs, few stomata, leaves reduced to spines, succulent water storage
formulas.note: Examples: cactus, marram grass, pineapple (CAM).

shortcuts.name: Potometer with r² first
shortcuts.rule: Square the radius, multiply by distance, then by π ≈ 3.14, then divide by time.
shortcuts.example: Radius 0.5 mm, bubble moves 30 mm in 5 min: 0.25 × 30 = 7.5, × π ≈ 23.6 mm³, ÷ 5 ≈ 4.7 mm³ min⁻¹.

shortcuts.name: Ringing experiment reading
shortcuts.rule: Removing a ring of bark removes phloem but leaves xylem: above the ring sugars pile up (swelling), below the ring tissues starve; the leaves do not wilt because water still flows.
shortcuts.example: 'After ringing, the stem swells above the cut. Why?' Sucrose moving down in the phloem cannot pass the ring and accumulates.

shortcuts.name: Only humidity slows it
shortcuts.rule: 'Hot, Bright, Windy, Dry → faster'; humidity is the one factor where an increase slows transpiration.
shortcuts.example: 'Which condition gives the lowest transpiration: hot, windy, humid or still?' → humid (and still).

shortcuts.name: Capillarity limit check
shortcuts.rule: Plug values in powers of ten to show capillarity alone is too small for tall trees.

shortcuts.name: Bundle layout rule
shortcuts.rule: In a dicot stem the xylem is on the inside and phloem on the outside of each bundle, arranged in a ring; in a root xylem forms a central star with phloem between its arms.
shortcuts.example: 'In a dicot stem section, which tissue is nearer the epidermis in a vascular bundle?' → phloem.

traps: Saying phloem cells are dead or xylem vessels are living; it is the reverse.
Saying a potometer measures transpiration exactly; it measures water uptake, some of which is used in photosynthesis and cell turgor.
Saying transpiration is useless water loss; it pulls up water and minerals and cools the leaf.
Forgetting that guard cells contain chloroplasts while other epidermal cells do not.
Saying phloem moves sugars only downward; translocation goes from source to sink in either direction.
nsmqTips: When asked to explain the ascent of sap, name all three: transpiration pull (cohesion–tension), root pressure, capillarity — and say transpiration pull is the main one.
Aphid stylets are used to collect pure phloem sap; this is a common 'how do scientists know' question.
Guttation (loss of liquid water through hydathodes) is caused by root pressure, usually at night or in humid conditions.
Know the dyes: eosin or red ink in water moves up the xylem, showing its position in a cut stem.

topics.summary: Excretion removes metabolic wastes such as CO₂, urea and excess salts; osmoregulation keeps the water and solute balance of body fluids steady. NSMQ asks about nephron structure, ADH, urea formation and which waste suits which habitat.
keyIdeas: Excretion removes waste made by metabolism; egestion removes undigested food, so faeces are mostly egested, not excreted (bile pigments are the exception).
Urea is made in the liver by deamination of excess amino acids and the ornithine cycle; the kidney only filters it out.
The nephron works by ultrafiltration at the glomerulus, selective reabsorption (mainly in the PCT) and water reabsorption controlled by ADH in the DCT and collecting duct.
All glucose and amino acids in the filtrate are normally reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
The loop of Henle builds a salt gradient in the medulla; a longer loop allows more concentrated urine.
ADH is made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary, and makes the collecting duct more permeable to water.
Freshwater protozoa such as Amoeba and Paramecium use contractile vacuoles to pump out excess water.
Plants excrete through stomata and lenticels, and by leaf fall, bark shedding and storing wastes such as latex, tannins and crystals.

formulas.name: Urea formation (net)
formulas.formula: 2NH₃ + CO₂ → CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O
formulas.note: Ornithine cycle in liver cells; uses ATP. NH₃ comes from deamination.

formulas.name: Deamination
formulas.formula: amino acid → keto acid + NH₃
formulas.note: Liver; the keto acid can be respired or turned into glucose or fat.

formulas.name: Nephron pathway
formulas.formula: glomerulus/Bowman's capsule → PCT → loop of Henle → DCT → collecting duct → ureter
formulas.note: Filtrate order; used in 'trace the path' questions.

formulas.name: Typical kidney figures
formulas.formula: GFR ≈ 125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day; urine ≈ 1.5 L/day
formulas.note: About 99% of filtered water is reabsorbed.

formulas.name: Renal clearance
formulas.formula: C = (U × V) / P
formulas.note: U = urine concentration, V = urine flow rate, P = plasma concentration. Clearance of inulin ≈ GFR.

formulas.name: Excretory organs and products
formulas.formula: Kidney: urea, salts, water; Lungs: CO₂, water vapour; Skin: sweat (water, salts, a little urea); Liver: bile pigments
formulas.note: Classic matching question.

formulas.name: Nitrogenous waste vs habitat
formulas.formula: Ammonia: most aquatic animals, bony fish, tadpoles; Urea: mammals, adult amphibians, sharks; Uric acid: birds, reptiles, insects
formulas.note: Toxicity and water needed: ammonia > urea > uric acid.

formulas.name: Hormones of water and salt balance
formulas.formula: ADH → more water reabsorbed; Aldosterone (adrenal cortex) → more Na⁺ reabsorbed in DCT and collecting duct
formulas.note: Both act on the distal nephron.

shortcuts.name: Percent reabsorbed
shortcuts.rule: Reabsorbed % = (filtered − urine)/filtered × 100; with 180 L filtered, each 1.8 L of urine is 1%.
shortcuts.example: 180 L filtered, 1.8 L urine: 1.8/180 = 1% excreted, so 99% reabsorbed.

shortcuts.name: Clearance equals GFR test
shortcuts.rule: If C = U × V / P comes out ≈ 125 mL/min, the substance is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted (like inulin). Lower → reabsorbed; higher → secreted.
shortcuts.example: U = 10 mg/mL, V = 1.25 mL/min, P = 0.1 mg/mL: C = 12.5/0.1 = 125 mL/min, so it behaves like inulin.

shortcuts.name: Water supply decides the waste
shortcuts.rule: Lots of water → ammonia; water must be saved → urea; very little water or a shelled egg → uric acid.
shortcuts.example: Bird embryo inside a shelled egg: cannot flush ammonia, so it makes insoluble uric acid.

shortcuts.name: Fish mnemonic: fresh pees, salt drinks
shortcuts.rule: Freshwater bony fish gain water: drink little, make lots of dilute urine, take in salt at the gills. Marine bony fish lose water: drink sea water, make little urine, pump salt out at the gills.
shortcuts.example: Tilapia in Lake Volta: large volume of dilute urine. A marine tuna: little concentrated urine.

shortcuts.name: ADH direction check
shortcuts.rule: Blood too concentrated → ADH up → small volume of concentrated urine. Blood too dilute, or alcohol/caffeine → ADH down → large dilute urine.
shortcuts.example: After a salty kenkey-and-fish meal without water, ADH rises and urine becomes dark and scanty.

shortcuts.name: Long loop, desert animal
shortcuts.rule: The longer the loop of Henle (thicker medulla), the more concentrated the urine.
shortcuts.example: Desert kangaroo rat has very long loops, so it can survive with almost no drinking water.

traps: Saying urea is made in the kidney; it is made in the liver.
Calling faeces an excretory product; they are egested (only bile pigments in them are excretory).
Saying ADH is made in the pituitary; it is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
Saying glucose is normally present in urine; its presence signals diabetes mellitus.
Giving marine protozoa contractile vacuoles as the main example; it is freshwater protozoa that need them.
nsmqTips: For 'which part of the nephron' questions, link the process: ultrafiltration → glomerulus, glucose reabsorption → PCT, salt gradient → loop of Henle, ADH action → collecting duct.
Riddles often describe the organ: 'I am made of about a million nephrons' → kidney.
When asked for the excretory product of an animal, think of its habitat and whether it lays shelled eggs.

topics.summary: The nervous system carries fast electrical impulses from receptors to effectors, with the brain and spinal cord as the control centre. NSMQ often tests the reflex arc, the action potential, brain regions and the structure and defects of the eye and ear.
keyIdeas: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; nerves outside them form the peripheral nervous system.
A neurone at rest has a potential of about −70 mV, inside negative, kept by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and leaky K⁺ channels.
An action potential is all-or-none: Na⁺ rushes in (depolarisation), then K⁺ leaves (repolarisation).
Myelin sheath and nodes of Ranvier allow saltatory conduction, which is much faster.
Synapses pass the impulse one way only, because neurotransmitter (e.g. acetylcholine) is released only from the presynaptic knob.
Rods work in dim light and give black-and-white vision; cones need bright light and give colour; the fovea has only cones; the blind spot has no receptors.
For near vision the ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes fatter.
The cochlea detects sound; the semicircular canals detect head rotation; the utricle and saccule detect head position.

formulas.name: Key membrane potentials
formulas.formula: Resting ≈ −70 mV; threshold ≈ −55 mV; peak ≈ +30 to +40 mV
formulas.note: Values vary a little between textbooks; −70 mV is the standard answer.

formulas.name: Sodium–potassium pump
formulas.formula: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP
formulas.note: Makes the inside negative relative to outside.

formulas.name: Reflex arc
formulas.formula: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (CNS) → motor neurone → effector
formulas.note: Spinal reflexes such as the knee jerk; the knee jerk itself has no relay neurone.

formulas.name: Conduction speed
formulas.formula: v = distance / time
formulas.note: Myelinated fibres up to about 100 m/s; non-myelinated about 0.5–2 m/s.

formulas.name: Lens power
formulas.formula: P = 1/f (f in metres), unit dioptre D
formulas.note: Converging (convex) lens has positive P; diverging (concave) has negative P.

formulas.name: Brain regions
formulas.formula: Cerebrum: thinking, memory, voluntary action; Cerebellum: balance and muscle coordination; Medulla oblongata: breathing, heart rate; Hypothalamus: temperature, water balance, hunger
formulas.note: Most asked matching set.

formulas.name: Path of sound
formulas.formula: pinna → ear canal → eardrum → malleus → incus → stapes → oval window → cochlea → auditory nerve
formulas.note: The ossicles amplify the vibration.

formulas.name: Path of light
formulas.formula: cornea → aqueous humour → pupil → lens → vitreous humour → retina → optic nerve
formulas.note: Most refraction happens at the cornea; the image is real and inverted.

shortcuts.name: Reaction time from speed
shortcuts.rule: Time = distance/speed; 1 m at 50 m/s is 0.02 s (20 ms). Halve the speed, double the time.
shortcuts.example: Toe to spinal cord 1 m at 50 m/s = 0.02 s; on a 1 m/s unmyelinated fibre it would take 1 s.

shortcuts.name: Myopia = Minus lens
shortcuts.rule: Short sight (myopia): eyeball too long, image in front of retina → concave lens (negative power). Long sight (hypermetropia): image behind retina → convex lens (positive power).
shortcuts.example: Concave lens of focal length 0.5 m: P = 1/(−0.5) = −2 D, prescribed for short sight.

shortcuts.name: Circular closes, radial opens
shortcuts.rule: Bright light: circular iris muscles contract → pupil constricts. Dim light: radial muscles contract → pupil dilates.
shortcuts.example: Walking from a dark cinema into sunlight: circular muscles contract, pupils become small.

shortcuts.name: Near = muscles work
shortcuts.rule: Near object needs a fat lens: ciliary muscles CONTRACT, ligaments SLACKEN. Far object: ciliary muscles relax, ligaments taut, lens thin.
shortcuts.example: Reading a phone at 25 cm: ciliary muscles contracted; looking at a far-off goalpost: relaxed.

shortcuts.name: Ossicles MIS order
shortcuts.rule: From eardrum inwards: Malleus (hammer), Incus (anvil), Stapes (stirrup). Stapes is the smallest bone in the body.
shortcuts.example: Which ossicle touches the oval window? The last in MIS: stapes.

shortcuts.name: Sympathetic = sprint
shortcuts.rule: Sympathetic (fight or flight) speeds the heart, dilates pupils and bronchioles, slows digestion; parasympathetic (rest and digest) does the opposite.
shortcuts.example: A student about to face a quiz: sympathetic → fast heartbeat, dry mouth, wide pupils.

traps: Saying ciliary muscles relax for near vision; they contract.
Confusing cerebellum (balance) with cerebrum (thinking).
Saying the blind spot has only rods; it has no receptors at all.
Saying impulses can cross synapses in both directions.
Saying a stronger stimulus gives a bigger action potential; it gives more frequent impulses of the same size.
nsmqTips: Riddles about a 'part of the brain damaged by alcohol causing staggering' point to the cerebellum.
For eye defects, state both the cause (eyeball shape or lens) and the correcting lens type.
Learn the eye and ear pathways as fixed strings; 'trace the path' questions reward speed.

topics.summary: Hormones are chemical messengers made by ductless (endocrine) glands and carried in the blood to target organs; homeostasis is the keeping of a steady internal environment, mostly by negative feedback.
