NSMQ tests glands and their hormones, deficiency disorders, blood-sugar and temperature control, and plant hormones.
keyIdeas: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood; the effect is slower and longer-lasting than nerves.
The pituitary is the 'master gland' and is itself controlled by the hypothalamus.
Insulin (β cells of the islets of Langerhans) lowers blood glucose; glucagon (α cells) raises it.
Negative feedback reverses a change; positive feedback amplifies it (e.g. oxytocin during labour).
The hypothalamus is the body's thermostat and keeps core temperature near 37 °C.
Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla prepares the body for fight or flight; the adrenal cortex makes aldosterone and cortisol.
Thyroxine needs iodine and controls metabolic rate.
Plants use hormones too: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid and ethylene.

formulas.name: Glucose regulation
formulas.formula: High glucose → insulin → glucose → glycogen (liver, muscle); Low glucose → glucagon → glycogen → glucose
formulas.note: Both from the pancreas.

formulas.name: Negative feedback loop
formulas.formula: change → receptor → control centre → effector → response opposes change
formulas.note: Applies to temperature, glucose, water.

formulas.name: Normal set points
formulas.formula: Core temperature ≈ 37 °C; fasting blood glucose ≈ 4–6 mmol/L (about 70–100 mg per 100 mL); blood pH ≈ 7.4
formulas.note: Common one-word answers.

formulas.name: Pituitary hormones
formulas.formula: Anterior: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin; Posterior: ADH, oxytocin
formulas.note: Posterior hormones are made in the hypothalamus.

formulas.name: Other glands
formulas.formula: Thyroid: thyroxine; Parathyroid: parathormone (raises blood Ca²⁺); Adrenal medulla: adrenaline; Adrenal cortex: aldosterone, cortisol; Testis: testosterone; Ovary: oestrogen, progesterone
formulas.note: Matching set.

formulas.name: Plant hormones
formulas.formula: Auxin: cell elongation, tropisms, apical dominance; Gibberellin: stem elongation, germination; Cytokinin: cell division; Abscisic acid: stomatal closure, dormancy; Ethylene: fruit ripening, abscission
formulas.note: Ethylene is a gas.

formulas.name: Temperature control
formulas.formula: Too hot: vasodilation, sweating, hairs flat; Too cold: vasoconstriction, shivering, hairs erect
formulas.note: Effectors are skin arterioles, sweat glands, erector muscles, skeletal muscles.

shortcuts.name: Child vs adult disorder pairs
shortcuts.rule: GH excess: child → gigantism, adult → acromegaly; GH lack in child → dwarfism. Thyroxine lack: child → cretinism, adult → myxoedema; iodine lack → goitre.
shortcuts.example: Adult whose hands, feet and jaw keep enlarging: excess GH after growth plates close → acromegaly.

shortcuts.name: Insulin puts glucose IN
shortcuts.rule: Insulin moves glucose INto cells and storage (lowers it); glucaGON is called when glucose is GONe (raises it).
shortcuts.example: Student skips breakfast, glucose falls → glucagon from α cells → liver breaks glycogen to glucose.

shortcuts.name: Two diabetes decider
shortcuts.rule: Sweet urine (glucose present) → diabetes mellitus (insulin problem). Large volume of dilute urine with no glucose → diabetes insipidus (ADH problem).
shortcuts.example: Patient passes 10 L of watery urine a day, no glucose: diabetes insipidus.

shortcuts.name: Hot vs cold mirror
shortcuts.rule: Every hot response has an opposite cold response: dilate/constrict, sweat/no sweat, hairs flat/erect, plus shivering only in cold.
shortcuts.example: On a cold Harmattan morning: vasoconstriction, hairs erect (goose bumps), shivering.

shortcuts.name: Auxin bends toward light
shortcuts.rule: Auxin moves to the shaded side; in shoots it speeds elongation there, so the shoot curves toward light. In roots high auxin slows growth, so the lower side grows less and the root bends down.
shortcuts.example: Seedling on a windowsill: auxin collects on the side away from the window, so it bends toward the window.

shortcuts.name: Plant hormone mnemonic ACE-GA
shortcuts.rule: Auxin, Cytokinin, Ethylene, Gibberellin, Abscisic acid. Ripening = Ethylene; dormancy and closing stomata = Abscisic acid; tall dwarf peas = Gibberellin.
shortcuts.example: Unripe bananas ripen faster in a bag with a ripe one: ethylene released by the ripe fruit.

traps: Confusing glucagon (hormone) with glycogen (storage polysaccharide).
Saying adrenaline comes from the adrenal cortex; it is the medulla.
Saying hormones travel in ducts; endocrine glands are ductless.
Thinking all feedback is negative; oxytocin in childbirth is positive feedback.
Saying sweating cools by removing heat with the water itself; cooling is by evaporation (latent heat).
nsmqTips: Expect 'name the gland and the hormone' riddles: 'I am the master gland at the base of the brain' → pituitary.
For deficiency questions, always check age: the same hormone gives different named disorders in children and adults.
Plant hormone questions are usually one-word: give the hormone, not a description.

topics.summary: Skeletons support the body, protect organs and act with muscles to produce movement; plants are supported by turgor and thickened tissues. NSMQ tests bones and vertebrae, joints, levers, antagonistic muscles and the sliding filament model.
keyIdeas: Three skeleton types: hydrostatic (earthworm), exoskeleton (arthropods, chitin) and endoskeleton (vertebrates).
The adult human skeleton has 206 bones and is divided into axial (skull, vertebrae, ribs, sternum) and appendicular (limbs and girdles).
Muscles can only pull; they work in antagonistic pairs, e.g. biceps flexes and triceps extends the elbow.
Tendons join muscle to bone and are inelastic; ligaments join bone to bone and are slightly elastic.
Synovial joints contain cartilage and synovial fluid to reduce friction.
In the sliding filament model, myosin heads pull actin filaments using ATP after Ca²⁺ is released, so the sarcomere shortens.
Plants are supported by turgid parenchyma, collenchyma (living, cellulose-thickened) and sclerenchyma and xylem (dead, lignified).

formulas.name: Bone count
formulas.formula: Adult human: 206 bones; newborn about 270–300
formulas.note: Bones fuse during growth.

formulas.name: Vertebral formula
formulas.formula: Cervical 7 + Thoracic 12 + Lumbar 5 + Sacral 5 (fused) + Coccygeal 4 (fused) = 33
formulas.note: Atlas C1 allows nodding; axis C2 (odontoid process) allows rotation.

formulas.name: Principle of moments
formulas.formula: effort × effort distance = load × load distance (about the fulcrum)
formulas.note: Limb levers; forearm lifting is a class 3 lever.

formulas.name: Joint types
formulas.formula: Ball-and-socket: shoulder, hip; Hinge: elbow, knee, fingers; Pivot: atlas–axis; Gliding: wrist, ankle bones; Fixed: skull sutures
formulas.note: Classic matching.

formulas.name: Sarcomere changes on contraction
formulas.formula: I band and H zone shorten; A band stays the same; Z lines move closer
formulas.note: Filaments do not shorten; they slide.

formulas.name: Muscle types
formulas.formula: Skeletal: striated, voluntary, multinucleate; Smooth: unstriated, involuntary (gut, blood vessels); Cardiac: striated, involuntary, branched, never tires
formulas.note: Cardiac muscle is myogenic.

formulas.name: Limb bones
formulas.formula: Arm: humerus, then radius (thumb side) and ulna; Leg: femur, then tibia (shin) and fibula; Patella = kneecap
formulas.note: Femur is the longest bone; stapes the smallest.

shortcuts.name: Lever effort in one line
shortcuts.rule: Effort = load × (load distance / effort distance).
shortcuts.example: Biceps attaches 4 cm from elbow, 10 N ball held 32 cm from elbow: effort = 10 × 32/4 = 80 N.

shortcuts.name: Lever class: F-L-E in the middle
shortcuts.rule: Class 1: Fulcrum in middle; Class 2: Load in middle; Class 3: Effort in middle (1-2-3 = F-L-E).
shortcuts.example: Nodding head: fulcrum (atlas joint) between face weight and neck muscles → class 1. Standing on tiptoe: load in middle → class 2.

shortcuts.name: Vertebrae meal times
shortcuts.rule: Breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5: cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5; then 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal.
shortcuts.example: How many vertebrae carry ribs? Thoracic = 12.

shortcuts.name: Spot the vertebra
shortcuts.rule: Holes in transverse processes (vertebrarterial canals) → cervical; rib facets and long downward spine → thoracic; big heavy centrum with wide processes → lumbar; fused with wings → sacrum.
shortcuts.example: Specimen with facets for ribs on the centrum: thoracic vertebra.

shortcuts.name: HI shrink, A stays
shortcuts.rule: On contraction the H zone and I band shrink; the A band (length of myosin) is constant.
shortcuts.example: Sarcomere shortens from 2.5 µm to 2.0 µm: A band unchanged, I band and H zone both narrower.

shortcuts.name: Ligament Links, Tendon Tethers
shortcuts.rule: Ligament links bone to bone; Tendon tethers muscle to bone.
shortcuts.example: Achilles tendon joins calf muscle to heel bone; a sprained ankle is torn ligament.

traps: Saying muscles push; they only pull.
Mixing up tendon and ligament.
Saying actin and myosin shorten during contraction; they slide past each other.
Saying collenchyma is lignified; it is living with extra cellulose. Sclerenchyma is lignified and dead.
Counting the sacrum and coccyx as one bone each without noting they are fused vertebrae (5 and 4).
nsmqTips: Riddles: 'I am the only bone in the body not jointed to another bone' → hyoid.
For lever problems, find the fulcrum first (usually the joint), then apply the moments rule mentally.
Vertebra identification questions describe a single feature; memorise one unique feature per region.

topics.summary: Reproduction produces new individuals, asexually by mitosis or sexually by fusion of gametes made by meiosis. NSMQ asks about the menstrual cycle hormones, gametogenesis, flower structure, pollination, double fertilisation and embryo development.
keyIdeas: Asexual reproduction gives genetically identical offspring; sexual reproduction gives variation through meiosis and random fertilisation.
In humans, sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules, stored in the epididymis; fertilisation normally happens in the oviduct.
FSH stimulates follicle growth; a surge of LH triggers ovulation; the corpus luteum secretes progesterone to maintain the uterine lining.
The placenta exchanges food, oxygen and wastes and secretes hormones, but maternal and fetal blood do not mix.
In flowering plants, the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
Double fertilisation is unique to flowering plants: one male nucleus fuses with the egg, the other with two polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm.
Self-pollination reduces variation; cross-pollination increases it.

formulas.name: Chromosome numbers in humans
formulas.formula: Gametes n = 23; zygote and body cells 2n = 46
formulas.note: Meiosis halves the number; fertilisation restores it.

formulas.name: Menstrual cycle timing
formulas.formula: Cycle ≈ 28 days; menstruation days 1–5; ovulation ≈ day 14
formulas.note: Luteal phase is about 14 days in most cycles.

formulas.name: Gametogenesis output
formulas.formula: 1 primary spermatocyte → 4 sperm; 1 primary oocyte → 1 ovum + polar bodies (up to 3)
formulas.note: Oogenesis keeps most cytoplasm in one cell.

formulas.name: Double fertilisation
formulas.formula: male nucleus + egg → zygote (2n); male nucleus + 2 polar nuclei → endosperm (3n)
formulas.note: Flowering plants only.

formulas.name: Flower to fruit
formulas.formula: Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit; integuments → testa; ovary wall → pericarp; zygote → embryo
formulas.note: Standard 'what becomes what' set.

formulas.name: Germ layers
formulas.formula: Ectoderm: skin, nervous system; Mesoderm: muscle, bone, blood, kidneys; Endoderm: gut lining, lungs, liver, pancreas
formulas.note: Triploblastic animals.

formulas.name: Gestation
formulas.formula: Human ≈ 40 weeks (280 days) counted from the last menstrual period, ≈ 38 weeks from fertilisation
formulas.note: Implantation about 6–7 days after fertilisation.

shortcuts.name: Ovulation day from cycle length
shortcuts.rule: Ovulation ≈ cycle length − 14 (the luteal phase is fairly fixed).
shortcuts.example: A 32-day cycle: ovulation ≈ day 32 − 14 = day 18.

shortcuts.name: Count gametes from cells
shortcuts.rule: Males: ×4. Females: ×1 functional ovum.
shortcuts.example: 50 primary spermatocytes → 200 sperm; 50 primary oocytes → 50 ova.

shortcuts.name: Plant ploidy table
shortcuts.rule: If n is given: pollen, egg, embryo sac nuclei = n; zygote, embryo, testa, pericarp = 2n; endosperm = 3n.
shortcuts.example: Maize n = 10: endosperm has 30 chromosomes, embryo 20, pollen 10.

shortcuts.name: Germ layers: Ecto Exterior, Endo iNside
shortcuts.rule: Ectoderm makes the outside and nerves; Endoderm lines the inside tubes; Mesoderm makes the middle (muscle, bone, blood).
shortcuts.example: The lining of the stomach comes from endoderm; the brain from ectoderm.

shortcuts.name: Wind vs insect flower
shortcuts.rule: Wind: small, dull, no scent or nectar, long feathery stigmas and dangling anthers, light pollen in large amounts. Insect: the opposite.
shortcuts.example: Maize tassels and grass: wind-pollinated. Hibiscus with bright petals and nectar: insect-pollinated.

shortcuts.name: LH = Launch the egg
shortcuts.rule: FSH Feeds the Follicle; LH Launches the egg (ovulation); Progesterone Protects the Pregnancy (keeps lining).
shortcuts.example: Which hormone surge occurs just before day 14? LH.

traps: Confusing pollination (transfer of pollen) with fertilisation (fusion of nuclei).
Saying FSH causes ovulation; it is the LH surge.
Saying endosperm is diploid; it is triploid.
Saying maternal and fetal blood mix in the placenta.
Saying sperm are made in the epididymis; they mature and are stored there.
nsmqTips: Riddles about 'I become the fruit' → ovary; 'I become the seed coat' → integument (testa).
Hormone graph questions: oestrogen peaks just before ovulation, progesterone peaks in the luteal phase.
When asked for ploidy, say the number, e.g. 'triploid, 3n'.

topics.summary: Classification sorts organisms into groups by shared features, and taxonomy names them using binomial nomenclature. NSMQ asks about the hierarchy of taxa, naming rules, kingdom features and the use of dichotomous keys.
keyIdeas: The hierarchy is Domain, Kingdom, Phylum (Division in plants), Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
Carolus Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature: Genus (capital) + species (small letter), italicised in print or underlined separately when handwritten.
A species is a group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
The five-kingdom system (Whittaker): Monera, Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
The three-domain system (Woese): Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya.
The more taxa two organisms share, the more closely related they are.
Viruses are not placed in any of the five kingdoms because they are not cells.

formulas.name: Taxonomic hierarchy
formulas.formula: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
formulas.note: Number of organisms in a group decreases down the list.

formulas.name: Binomial name
formulas.formula: Genus species, e.g. Homo sapiens, Zea mays, Plasmodium falciparum
formulas.note: After first use the genus may be shortened: H. sapiens.

formulas.name: Classification of humans
formulas.formula: Eukarya, Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, Homo, sapiens
formulas.note: Frequently asked in full.

formulas.name: Five kingdoms: key features
formulas.formula: Monera: prokaryotic; Protoctista: eukaryotic, mostly unicellular; Fungi: chitin walls, heterotrophic, spores; Plantae: cellulose walls, chlorophyll; Animalia: no walls, multicellular heterotrophs
formulas.note: Decide from cell wall and nutrition.

formulas.name: Dichotomous key
formulas.formula: Each step is a pair of contrasting statements, each leading to a name or to the next pair
formulas.note: Use visible, unchanging features.

formulas.name: Species test
formulas.formula: Same species ⇔ interbreed naturally to give fertile offspring
formulas.note: Horse × donkey → sterile mule, so different species.

shortcuts.name: Mnemonic for the ranks
shortcuts.rule: Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
shortcuts.example: Which rank lies between Class and Family? Order (Came Over For).

shortcuts.name: Shared rank implies all higher ranks
shortcuts.rule: If two organisms share a rank, they share every rank above it.
shortcuts.example: Lion Panthera leo and tiger Panthera tigris share the genus Panthera, so they must share family Felidae, order Carnivora and class Mammalia.

shortcuts.name: Couplets in a key
shortcuts.rule: A strictly dichotomous key that separates n organisms needs n − 1 couplets.
shortcuts.example: 8 insects to identify → 7 pairs of statements.

shortcuts.name: Kingdom by elimination
shortcuts.rule: No nucleus → Monera. Nucleus + chitin wall → Fungi. Nucleus + cellulose wall + chlorophyll and multicellular → Plantae. No wall, multicellular → Animalia. Otherwise mainly unicellular eukaryote → Protoctista.
shortcuts.example: Amoeba: nucleus, no wall, single cell → Protoctista.

shortcuts.name: Spot a wrongly written name
shortcuts.rule: Check three things: genus capitalised, species lower case, both italic or each underlined separately.
shortcuts.example: 'homo Sapiens' is wrong twice; correct is Homo sapiens.

traps: Capitalising the species name (sapiens, not Sapiens).
Using 'phylum' for plants in strict answers; plants traditionally use 'division'.
Putting fungi in the plant kingdom; they lack chlorophyll and have chitin.
Calling the genus name alone the scientific name of a species.
Placing viruses in Monera.
nsmqTips: Riddles: 'I am the father of taxonomy' → Carolus Linnaeus.
If asked to arrange taxa, start with the broadest (Kingdom or Domain) unless asked otherwise.
When asked why two organisms are different species, use the fertile-offspring test.

topics.summary: Animals are grouped into invertebrate phyla and the vertebrate classes of the phylum Chordata by body plan, symmetry, skeleton and other features. NSMQ loves identification riddles, arthropod classes, life cycles and the features of each vertebrate class.
keyIdeas: Cnidaria (Hydra, jellyfish) are radially symmetrical and diploblastic; most other phyla are triploblastic and bilaterally symmetrical.
Platyhelminthes (flatworms, tapeworm, liver fluke) are flat and unsegmented; Nematoda (roundworms, Ascaris) are round and unsegmented; Annelida (earthworm, leech) are segmented.
Mollusca (snail, octopus) have a soft body, a muscular foot and often a shell; Echinodermata (starfish) are marine with tube feet.
Arthropods have jointed legs, a chitin exoskeleton and must moult to grow.
Chordates have, at some stage, a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail.
Birds and mammals are endothermic (warm-blooded); fish, amphibians and reptiles are ectothermic.
Amphibians lay eggs in water; reptiles and birds lay shelled (amniotic) eggs on land.

formulas.name: Arthropod classes
formulas.formula: Insects: 3 body parts, 6 legs, 1 pair antennae; Arachnids: 2 parts, 8 legs, no antennae; Crustaceans: 2 pairs antennae, many with 10 legs; Myriapods: many segments with legs
formulas.note: Centipede 1 pair of legs per segment; millipede 2 pairs.

formulas.name: Heart chambers
formulas.formula: Fish 2; Amphibians 3; Reptiles 3 (crocodiles 4); Birds 4; Mammals 4
formulas.note: Fish have single circulation; others double.

formulas.name: Insect metamorphosis
formulas.formula: Complete: egg → larva → pupa → adult (butterfly, housefly, mosquito, beetle); Incomplete: egg → nymph → adult (cockroach, grasshopper, termite)
formulas.note: Moulting is controlled by ecdysone.

formulas.name: Vertebrate class features
formulas.formula: Fish: scales, gills, fins; Amphibians: moist skin, larva in water; Reptiles: dry scales, shelled eggs; Birds: feathers, beak, hollow bones; Mammals: hair, mammary glands, diaphragm, pinna
formulas.note: One unique feature is enough to identify.

formulas.name: Respiratory surfaces
formulas.formula: Insects: tracheae; Spiders: book lungs; Fish: gills; Earthworm: skin; Frog: skin, buccal cavity, lungs; Birds: lungs with air sacs
formulas.note: Common matching.

formulas.name: Symmetry and layers
formulas.formula: Radial + diploblastic: Cnidaria; Bilateral + triploblastic: flatworms onward; Echinoderm adults radial (pentaradial) but larvae bilateral
formulas.note: Sponges (Porifera) have no true tissues.

shortcuts.name: Count the legs
shortcuts.rule: 6 legs → insect; 8 → arachnid; 10 → decapod crustacean; dozens → myriapod.
shortcuts.example: Tick with 8 legs → arachnid, not insect; crab with 10 legs → crustacean.

shortcuts.name: Heart chambers 2-3-3-4-4
shortcuts.rule: Going fish → amphibian → reptile → bird → mammal the chambers go 2, 3, 3, 4, 4; crocodile is the exception reptile with 4.
shortcuts.example: How many chambers in a lizard's heart? Reptile → 3.

shortcuts.name: Pupa means complete
shortcuts.rule: If a pupa stage is mentioned it is complete metamorphosis; Nymph means No pupa (incomplete).
shortcuts.example: Grasshopper young look like small adults without wings → nymphs → incomplete metamorphosis.

shortcuts.name: Hair or milk means mammal
shortcuts.rule: Any animal with hair or mammary glands is a mammal, whatever its habitat or flying ability.
shortcuts.example: Bat flies, whale swims, but both suckle young → mammals.

shortcuts.name: Larva names
shortcuts.rule: Frog → tadpole; butterfly → caterpillar; housefly → maggot; mosquito → wriggler; beetle → grub.
shortcuts.example: 'A legless larva that feeds on rotting meat' → maggot of the housefly.

traps: Calling spiders, ticks and scorpions insects; they are arachnids.
Calling starfish and jellyfish fish.
Saying all reptiles have a 3-chambered heart without noting crocodiles.
Calling the snail an annelid; it is a mollusc.
Saying the earthworm self-fertilises; it is hermaphrodite but cross-fertilises.
nsmqTips: Identification riddles usually give 3–4 clues; jump in at the first unique one (e.g. 'book lungs' → spider).
Know local examples: tilapia (fish), agama lizard (reptile), giant African snail (mollusc), tsetse fly (insect).
When comparing classes, quote a feature that is truly unique, such as feathers for birds.

topics.summary: This topic covers the main plant groups, fungi, bacteria, viruses and protoctists, their structure, nutrition and reproduction. NSMQ asks about plant life cycles, monocot vs dicot features, fungal and bacterial features, bacterial growth and fermentation.
keyIdeas: Plant groups: bryophytes (mosses, no true vascular tissue), pteridophytes (ferns, vascular, spores), gymnosperms (naked seeds, cones) and angiosperms (flowers, seeds in fruits).
In mosses the gametophyte is dominant; in ferns and seed plants the sporophyte is dominant.
Fungi have chitin cell walls, are heterotrophic (saprophytic or parasitic), store glycogen and reproduce by spores; the body is a mycelium of hyphae.
Bacteria are prokaryotes with a peptidoglycan wall, no nucleus, 70S ribosomes, and often plasmids.
Viruses are non-cellular: a nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat; they reproduce only inside host cells.
Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses.
Microorganisms are used in bread (yeast, CO₂), alcohol (yeast, ethanol), yoghurt (Lactobacillus) and nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium).

formulas.name: Photosynthesis
formulas.formula: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (light, chlorophyll)
formulas.note: The O₂ comes from water.

formulas.name: Alcoholic fermentation (yeast)
formulas.formula: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
formulas.note: Gives 2 ATP per glucose; used in brewing and baking.

formulas.name: Lactic acid fermentation
formulas.formula: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2CH₃CH(OH)COOH
formulas.note: Lactobacillus in yoghurt; also in human muscle.

formulas.name: Bacterial growth
formulas.formula: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, n = t / g
formulas.note: N₀ initial number, g generation (doubling) time, t elapsed time; valid in the log phase.

formulas.name: Bacterial shapes
formulas.formula: Coccus: sphere; Bacillus: rod; Spirillum: spiral; Vibrio: comma
formulas.note: Staphylo- clusters, Strepto- chains, Diplo- pairs.

formulas.name: Gram stain
formulas.formula: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, stains purple; Gram-negative: thin wall + outer membrane, stains pink/red
formulas.note: Gram-negatives are generally more resistant to penicillin.

formulas.name: Monocot vs dicot
formulas.formula: Monocot: 1 cotyledon, parallel veins, fibrous roots, scattered vascular bundles, flower parts in 3s; Dicot: 2 cotyledons, net veins, taproot, bundles in a ring, parts in 4s or 5s
formulas.note: Maize, rice, oil palm = monocots; beans, cocoa, mango = dicots.

shortcuts.name: Doubling with powers of 2
shortcuts.rule: Count generations n = t/g, then use 2ⁿ; remember 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≈ 1000.
shortcuts.example: One cell, doubling every 20 min, after 2 h: n = 6, so 2⁶ = 64 cells. After 200 min: 2¹⁰ ≈ 1000 cells.

shortcuts.name: Gram Positive = Purple
shortcuts.rule: Remember PP: Positive → Purple. Pink → negative.
shortcuts.example: A pink rod after Gram staining: Gram-negative bacillus (e.g. E. coli).

shortcuts.name: Prefix + shape = name
shortcuts.rule: Prefix gives arrangement, ending gives shape: Strepto + coccus = chains of spheres; Staphylo + coccus = grape-like clusters.
shortcuts.example: Staphylococcus aureus seen as clusters of round cells.

shortcuts.name: Moss Mostly gametophyte
shortcuts.rule: Moss = Mostly gametophyte (green leafy plant is n); Fern Frond = sporophyte (2n).
shortcuts.example: Ploidy of the green leafy moss plant? Haploid (n).

shortcuts.name: Fungus decider
shortcuts.rule: No chlorophyll + chitin wall + spores + glycogen store → fungus, even if it looks like a plant.
shortcuts.example: Mushroom growing on a rotting log → fungus (saprophyte), not a plant.

shortcuts.name: Three-count monocot check
shortcuts.rule: Floral parts in multiples of 3 with parallel veins → monocot at once.
shortcuts.example: Lily with 6 petals and parallel veins → monocot.

traps: Saying antibiotics cure viral infections.
Calling yeast a bacterium; it is a unicellular fungus.
Calling blue-green algae true algae; they are cyanobacteria (prokaryotes).
Saying fungi store starch; they store glycogen.
Saying gymnosperms have fruits; their seeds are naked.
nsmqTips: Expect riddles on alternation of generations: state which generation is dominant.
Bacterial growth questions are designed for powers of 2; convert minutes to generations first.
For 'which organism is used to make…' questions, answer with the genus (Saccharomyces, Lactobacillus, Penicillium).

topics.summary: Ecology studies how organisms interact with each other and with their surroundings, including energy flow, nutrient cycles and population size. NSMQ often sets quick calculations on energy transfer, mark–release–recapture and quadrats, plus questions on the nitrogen cycle and species interactions.
keyIdeas: Energy flows one way through an ecosystem and is lost as heat; nutrients are recycled.
Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next, which limits food chains to about 4–5 levels.
Arrows in a food chain point from the organism eaten to the one eating it.
Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) release nutrients from dead matter.
Pyramids of numbers and biomass can be inverted; a pyramid of energy never is.
Population size changes by births and immigration minus deaths and emigration.
Major environmental issues include deforestation, galamsey water pollution, eutrophication, global warming and loss of biodiversity.

formulas.name: Ten percent rule
formulas.formula: Energy at next level ≈ 0.1 × energy at current level
formulas.note: Approximate; real values range about 5–20%.

formulas.name: Ecological efficiency
formulas.formula: Efficiency (%) = energy at higher level / energy at lower level × 100
formulas.note: Used with data from food chains.

formulas.name: Lincoln index (mark–release–recapture)
formulas.formula: N = (M × C) / R
formulas.note: M marked first, C caught second time, R recaptured marked. Assumes no births, deaths or migration and marks not lost.

formulas.name: Quadrat estimate
formulas.formula: Population ≈ mean per quadrat × (total area / quadrat area)
formulas.note: For plants and slow-moving animals.

formulas.name: Population change
formulas.formula: ΔN = (births + immigration) − (deaths + emigration)
formulas.note: Growth rate when divided by time.

formulas.name: Nitrogen cycle steps
formulas.formula: Fixation: N₂ → NH₃ (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, lightning); Nitrification: NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ (Nitrosomonas) → NO₃⁻ (Nitrobacter); Denitrification: NO₃⁻ → N₂ (Pseudomonas)
formulas.note: Plants absorb mainly nitrate.

formulas.name: Interactions
formulas.formula: Mutualism (+,+); Commensalism (+,0); Parasitism (+,−); Predation (+,−); Competition (−,−)
formulas.note: Sign pairs for the two species.

formulas.name: Carbon cycle
formulas.formula: CO₂ removed by photosynthesis; returned by respiration, decomposition and combustion
formulas.note: Burning fossil fuels raises atmospheric CO₂.

shortcuts.name: Shift the decimal for each level
shortcuts.rule: Each step up a food chain divides the energy by 10, so move the decimal point one place left per level.
shortcuts.example: Producers 10 000 kJ → primary 1000 → secondary 100 → tertiary 10 kJ.

shortcuts.name: Lincoln in your head
shortcuts.rule: Multiply the two catches, divide by the recaptured marked.
shortcuts.example: 40 snails marked; later 50 caught, 10 marked: N = 40 × 50 / 10 = 200 snails.

shortcuts.name: Quadrat scale-up
shortcuts.rule: Find the number of quadrats that fit the field, then multiply by the mean.
shortcuts.example: Mean 4 plants per 1 m² quadrat; field 50 m × 20 m = 1000 m², so ≈ 4000 plants.

shortcuts.name: Nitroso sooner, Nitrobacter better
shortcuts.rule: Nitrosomonas does the first step (to nitrite); Nitrobacter finishes the job (to nitrate). Pseudomonas puts N₂ back in the air.
shortcuts.example: Which bacterium converts nitrite to nitrate? Nitrobacter.

shortcuts.name: Sign test for relationships
shortcuts.rule: Ask: does each partner gain (+), lose (−) or neither (0)?
shortcuts.example: Rhizobium and legumes: both gain → mutualism. Tapeworm in human: + and − → parasitism. Cattle egret and cattle: egret gains, cattle unaffected → commensalism.

shortcuts.name: Spot an inverted pyramid
shortcuts.rule: One big producer feeding many small consumers inverts the number pyramid; fast-reproducing tiny producers (phytoplankton) can invert the biomass pyramid. Energy never inverts.
shortcuts.example: One mango tree supporting 500 caterpillars → inverted pyramid of numbers.

traps: Drawing food chain arrows the wrong way (they show energy flow to the eater).
Saying energy is recycled; only matter is.
Calling decomposers a trophic level in a simple food chain answer when the question wants producer/consumer levels.
Mixing up nitrification and nitrogen fixation.
Forgetting the Lincoln index assumptions when asked why the estimate may be wrong.
nsmqTips: Energy and Lincoln index questions are built for mental arithmetic; set up the product before you divide.
For nitrogen cycle riddles, name the genus of bacteria, not just 'bacteria'.
Give Ghanaian examples for environmental issues: galamsey, bush burning, deforestation, plastic waste.

topics.summary: Genetics explains how characteristics pass from parents to offspring through genes on chromosomes, following Mendel's laws and their extensions. NSMQ questions are quick probability problems, cross ratios, blood groups, sex-linkage, DNA base pairing and Hardy–Weinberg.
keyIdeas: A gene is a length of DNA coding for a polypeptide; alleles are different forms of the same gene.
Mendel's first law (segregation): the two alleles separate into different gametes. Second law (independent assortment): genes on different chromosomes assort independently.
Codominance shows both alleles (AB blood group); incomplete dominance gives a blend (red × white → pink four o'clock flowers).
X-linked recessive conditions (haemophilia, red–green colour blindness) are more common in males, who have only one X.
A test cross with the homozygous recessive reveals an unknown genotype.
DNA pairs A with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G with C (three); RNA has U instead of T.
A codon of three bases codes for one amino acid; there are 4³ = 64 codons.

formulas.name: Monohybrid F₂
formulas.formula: Phenotype 3 : 1; Genotype 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa
formulas.note: From Aa × Aa with complete dominance.

formulas.name: Dihybrid F₂
formulas.note: From AaBb × AaBb, genes unlinked.

formulas.name: Test cross results
formulas.formula: Aa × aa → 1 : 1; AA × aa → all dominant
formulas.note: Reveals whether a dominant-looking parent is a carrier.

formulas.name: Hardy–Weinberg
formulas.formula: p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1
formulas.note: p, q allele frequencies; q² = frequency of recessive phenotype; 2pq = carriers.

formulas.name: Gamete types
formulas.formula: Number of gamete types = 2ⁿ
formulas.note: n = number of heterozygous gene pairs (unlinked).

formulas.name: ABO blood group
formulas.formula: Iᴬ and Iᴮ codominant, i recessive; A: IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi; B: IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi; AB: IᴬIᴮ; O: ii
formulas.note: 4 phenotypes, 6 genotypes.

formulas.name: Chargaff's rule
formulas.formula: A = T and G = C, so A + G = T + C = 50%
formulas.note: Double-stranded DNA only.

formulas.name: Recombination frequency
formulas.formula: RF = recombinants / total offspring × 100%; 1% = 1 map unit (centimorgan)
formulas.note: Measures distance between linked genes; RF ≤ 50%.

shortcuts.name: Hardy–Weinberg from the rare phenotype
shortcuts.rule: Start from q² (the recessive phenotype), take √ for q, then p = 1 − q and carriers = 2pq.
shortcuts.example: 1 in 100 people has a recessive condition: q² = 0.01, q = 0.1, p = 0.9, carriers 2pq = 2 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.18 (18%).

shortcuts.name: Chargaff in one step
shortcuts.rule: Given one base %, its partner is equal, and the other two share what is left equally.

shortcuts.name: Multiply gene by gene
shortcuts.rule: For unlinked genes, find the probability for each gene separately and multiply.
shortcuts.example: AaBbCc × AaBbCc: P(aabbcc) = ¼ × ¼ × ¼ = 1/64. P(A_B_) from AaBb × AaBb = ¾ × ¾ = 9/16.

shortcuts.name: Carrier mother rule
shortcuts.rule: XᴴXʰ × XᴴY: half the sons affected, no daughters affected, half the daughters carriers.
shortcuts.example: Colour-blind carrier mother and normal father: chance a son is colour-blind = ½; chance any child is colour-blind = ¼.

shortcuts.name: Blood group exclusion
shortcuts.rule: O × O gives only O; an AB parent cannot have an O child; a child's Iᴬ or Iᴮ must come from a parent who has it.
shortcuts.example: Mother O, child B: the father must carry Iᴮ, so he is B or AB, never A or O.

shortcuts.name: Genotype count for multiple alleles
shortcuts.rule: With k alleles of one gene, number of genotypes = k(k + 1)/2.
shortcuts.example: ABO has 3 alleles: 3 × 4/2 = 6 genotypes.

traps: Expecting exact 3 : 1 in small samples; ratios are probabilities.
Saying males can be carriers of an X-linked recessive allele; they either have it or not.
Confusing codominance (both seen, e.g. AB) with incomplete dominance (blend, e.g. pink).
Using q² for carriers instead of 2pq.
Forgetting that each child's probability is independent of previous children.
nsmqTips: Most genetics questions resolve with fractions ½, ¼ and ¾; say the answer as a fraction.
For Hardy–Weinberg, always identify whether the given number is a phenotype frequency (q²) or allele frequency (q).
Riddles: 'father of genetics' → Gregor Mendel; 'organism he used' → garden pea, Pisum sativum.

topics.summary: Evolution is the change in heritable features of populations over many generations, explained mainly by natural selection. NSMQ asks about Darwin vs Lamarck, evidence for evolution, homologous and analogous structures, speciation and examples such as sickle-cell and antibiotic resistance.
keyIdeas: Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection: variation exists, more young are produced than survive, the best-adapted survive and reproduce, and their features are inherited.
Lamarck proposed use and disuse and the inheritance of acquired characteristics, which is not supported by evidence.
Evidence for evolution includes fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, molecular biology (DNA and protein sequences) and biogeography.
Homologous structures (pentadactyl limb) show divergent evolution; analogous structures (bird and insect wings) show convergent evolution.
New species form when populations are reproductively isolated, often by geography (allopatric speciation).
Populations evolve; individuals do not.
The sickle-cell allele persists in West Africa because heterozygotes are resistant to malaria (heterozygote advantage).

formulas.name: Radioactive decay for dating
formulas.formula: N = N₀ × (½)^(t / T½)
formulas.note: Carbon-14 half-life ≈ 5730 years; useful for remains up to about 50 000 years.

formulas.name: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium conditions
formulas.formula: Large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, no selection
formulas.note: If any fails, allele frequencies change, i.e. evolution occurs.

formulas.name: Natural selection outline
formulas.formula: Variation → overproduction → struggle for existence → survival of the fittest → inheritance → change over generations
formulas.note: Use this order in explanations.

formulas.name: Homologous vs analogous
formulas.formula: Homologous: same basic structure, different function; Analogous: different structure, same function
formulas.note: Arm, flipper, wing of bat = homologous; wings of bird and butterfly = analogous.

formulas.name: Types of selection
formulas.formula: Stabilising: favours the average; Directional: favours one extreme; Disruptive: favours both extremes
formulas.note: Birth weight in humans is stabilising.

formulas.name: Classic examples
formulas.formula: Peppered moth (industrial melanism); Darwin's finches (adaptive radiation); antibiotic-resistant bacteria; sickle-cell and malaria
formulas.note: Know one per idea.

shortcuts.name: Half-life counting
shortcuts.rule: Fraction left ½, ¼, ⅛, 1/16 → 1, 2, 3, 4 half-lives; multiply by 5730 years.
shortcuts.example: Bone with 25% of its original C-14 → 2 half-lives → 2 × 5730 = 11 460 years. 12.5% → 3 × 5730 = 17 190 years.

shortcuts.name: Lamarck or Darwin?
shortcuts.rule: If the explanation says the animal tried, used or stretched and passed that change on → Lamarck. If variation was already present and survivors bred → Darwin.
shortcuts.example: 'Giraffes stretched their necks and their young were born with longer necks' → Lamarck.

shortcuts.name: Same bones = homologous
shortcuts.rule: Same bone plan (humerus, radius, ulna, digits) → homologous, divergent. Same job, different build → analogous, convergent.
shortcuts.example: Human arm and whale flipper: same bones → homologous. Bat wing and butterfly wing: analogous.

shortcuts.name: Vestigial organ list
shortcuts.rule: Appendix, coccyx (tail bone), wisdom teeth, ear-moving muscles, plica semilunaris (remnant third eyelid).
shortcuts.example: 'Name a vestigial structure in humans' → appendix or coccyx.

shortcuts.name: Resistance is selected, not created
shortcuts.rule: The antibiotic does not cause resistance; resistant mutants already present survive and multiply.
shortcuts.example: Patient stops antibiotics early: surviving bacteria are the most resistant, so the next infection is harder to treat.

traps: Saying individuals evolve; populations evolve.
Saying 'fittest' means strongest; it means best at surviving and reproducing in that environment.
Saying mutations happen because the organism needs them; they are random.
Saying humans evolved from modern chimpanzees; they share a common ancestor.
Confusing homologous with analogous.
nsmqTips: Riddles: 'book published in 1859' → On the Origin of Species by Charles Darwin.
Explain natural selection in the fixed order: variation, competition, survival, reproduction, inheritance.
Use local examples: sickle-cell trait and malaria in Ghana, and insecticide resistance in mosquitoes.

topics.summary: This topic covers infectious diseases and their causes and vectors, the immune response, vaccination and nutrition-related disorders. NSMQ frequently asks for causative organisms, vectors, types of immunity and deficiency diseases, often with Ghanaian examples.
keyIdeas: Pathogens include viruses, bacteria, protozoa, fungi and parasitic worms.
Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium (P. falciparum is most deadly) and spread by the female Anopheles mosquito.
The first line of defence is skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid and lysozyme; phagocytes and inflammation follow.
Specific immunity uses lymphocytes: B cells make antibodies (as plasma cells); T cells kill infected cells and help B cells.
B cells mature in the bone marrow, T cells in the thymus; HIV attacks helper T (CD4) cells.
Vaccines give active artificial immunity by stimulating memory cells; ready-made antibodies give passive immunity.
Antibiotics kill or stop bacteria; they do not work on viruses.

formulas.name: Disease → cause → vector/spread
formulas.formula: Malaria: Plasmodium, female Anopheles; Sleeping sickness: Trypanosoma, tsetse fly; River blindness: Onchocerca volvulus, blackfly (Simulium); Bilharzia: Schistosoma, freshwater snail; Yellow fever: virus, Aedes mosquito
formulas.note: Core matching set.

formulas.name: Bacterial diseases
formulas.formula: Cholera: Vibrio cholerae; Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; Typhoid: Salmonella typhi; Tetanus: Clostridium tetani; Gonorrhoea: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
formulas.note: Treatable with antibiotics.

formulas.name: Viral diseases
formulas.formula: HIV/AIDS, measles, polio, hepatitis B, yellow fever, COVID-19, Ebola, chickenpox, rabies
formulas.note: Prevented mainly by vaccines and hygiene.

formulas.name: Types of immunity
formulas.formula: Active natural: after infection; Active artificial: vaccine; Passive natural: antibodies across placenta or in breast milk; Passive artificial: injected antiserum (e.g. antivenom)
formulas.note: Active = long-lasting with memory; passive = immediate but short.

formulas.name: Antibody structure
formulas.formula: Y-shaped protein: 2 heavy + 2 light chains joined by disulfide bonds; 2 antigen-binding sites
formulas.note: Made by plasma cells.

formulas.name: Deficiency diseases
formulas.formula: Vitamin A: night blindness; B₁: beriberi; C: scurvy; D: rickets; Iron: anaemia; Iodine: goitre; Protein: kwashiorkor; Protein + energy: marasmus
formulas.note: Frequently asked.

formulas.name: Body mass index
formulas.formula: BMI = mass (kg) / height² (m²)
formulas.note: 18.5–24.9 normal; 25–29.9 overweight; ≥ 30 obese.

formulas.name: Herd immunity threshold
formulas.formula: Fraction to immunise = 1 − 1/R₀
formulas.note: R₀ = average number infected by one case in a fully susceptible population.

shortcuts.name: BMI with a squared height
shortcuts.rule: Square the height first (1.6² = 2.56, 1.7² = 2.89, 1.8² = 3.24), then divide.

shortcuts.name: Herd immunity in one step
shortcuts.rule: Coverage needed = 1 − 1/R₀.

shortcuts.name: Active makes, passive takes
shortcuts.rule: If the body MAKES its own antibodies → active (memory). If antibodies are TAKEN ready-made → passive (no memory).
shortcuts.example: Antivenom after a snake bite → passive artificial. Baby breastfeeding → passive natural. Polio drops → active artificial.

shortcuts.name: Vector letter pairs
shortcuts.rule: Tsetse → Trypanosoma (T-T); Snail → Schistosoma (S-S); Blackfly → Blindness (B-B); Anopheles → Ague (old word for malaria).
shortcuts.example: Which vector spreads river blindness? Blackfly.

shortcuts.name: Vitamin cues
shortcuts.rule: A for eyes; B₁ for beriberi; C for citrus and scurvy (bleeding gums); D for daylight and bones (rickets).
shortcuts.example: Child with bowed legs and little sunlight exposure → vitamin D deficiency, rickets.

shortcuts.name: Kwashiorkor vs marasmus
shortcuts.rule: Swollen belly and oedema with some energy intake → kwashiorkor (protein lack). Wasted, 'skin and bones' → marasmus (energy and protein lack).
shortcuts.example: Weaned toddler on mainly cassava, with swollen legs and reddish hair → kwashiorkor.

traps: Saying the mosquito causes malaria; it is the vector, the cause is Plasmodium.
Saying male Anopheles transmit malaria; only females take blood meals.
Saying vaccines give passive immunity; they give active artificial immunity.
Saying antibiotics treat colds or flu; these are viral.
Treating HIV and AIDS as the same; HIV is the virus, AIDS the syndrome it causes.
nsmqTips: Questions often give a disease and ask for the causative organism and vector; answer both with genus names.
Riddles: 'I developed the first vaccine' → Edward Jenner (smallpox); 'I discovered penicillin' → Alexander Fleming.
Know the Ghana context: malaria, cholera outbreaks, Buruli ulcer (Mycobacterium ulcerans), guinea worm eradication (Dracunculus medinensis).
